The ability to deploy neural networks in real-world, safety-critical systems
is severely limited by the presence of adversarial examples: slightly perturbed
inputs that are misclassified by the network. In recent years, several
techniques have been proposed for increasing robustness to adversarial examples
--- and yet most of these have been quickly shown to be vulnerable to future
attacks. For example, over half of the defenses proposed by papers accepted at
ICLR 2018 have already been broken. We propose to address this difficulty
through formal verification techniques. We show how to construct provably
minimally distorted adversarial examples: given an arbitrary neural network and
input sample, we can construct adversarial examples which we prove are of
minimal distortion. Using this approach, we demonstrate that one of the recent
ICLR defense proposals, adversarial retraining, provably succeeds at increasing
the distortion required to construct adversarial examples by a factor of 4.2.
Rewrite this for me:
The practical use of neural networks in safety-critical applications is heavily constrained by adversarial examples—subtly altered inputs that cause misclassification. While numerous methods to enhance robustness have emerged in recent years, most are subsequently broken by new attacks. For instance, more than half of the defenses presented at ICLR 2018 have already been circumvented.

To tackle this persistent challenge, we employ formal verification. Our method generates provably minimally distorted adversarial examples: for any given network and input, we can construct perturbed inputs and formally prove they have the smallest possible distortion. Applying this technique, we verify that one recent ICLR defense, adversarial retraining, definitively increases the minimum distortion needed for an attack by a factor of 4.2. This provides a certified measure of improved robustness.

We propose a principled method for kernel learning, which relies on a
Fourier-analytic characterization of translation-invariant or
rotation-invariant kernels. Our method produces a sequence of feature maps,
iteratively refining the SVM margin. We provide rigorous guarantees for
optimality and generalization, interpreting our algorithm as online
equilibrium-finding dynamics in a certain two-player min-max game. Evaluations
on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate scalability and consistent
improvements over related random features-based methods.
Rewrite this for me: We introduce a principled kernel learning method based on a Fourier analysis of translation- or rotation-invariant kernels. It iteratively refines SVM feature maps to maximize the margin. The algorithm is formally interpreted as online equilibrium-finding in a min-max game, with guarantees for optimality and generalization. Tests on synthetic and real-world data show it scales well and consistently outperforms comparable random features methods.

input:
State-of-the-art deep reading comprehension models are dominated by recurrent
neural nets. Their sequential nature is a natural fit for language, but it also
precludes parallelization within an instances and often becomes the bottleneck
for deploying such models to latency critical scenarios. This is particularly
problematic for longer texts. Here we present a convolutional architecture as
an alternative to these recurrent architectures. Using simple dilated
convolutional units in place of recurrent ones, we achieve results comparable
to the state of the art on two question answering tasks, while at the same time
achieving up to two orders of magnitude speedups for question answering.
Rewrite this for me: Current top-performing models for deep reading comprehension rely heavily on recurrent neural networks. While their sequential processing aligns well with language, it prevents parallel computation within a single input. This often creates a performance bottleneck, especially for longer texts, making deployment in latency-sensitive applications difficult. We propose a convolutional architecture as an alternative. By employing basic dilated convolutional units instead of recurrent ones, we match state-of-the-art accuracy on two question answering benchmarks. Simultaneously, this approach delivers speed improvements of up to 100 times for question answering.

This report has several purposes. First, our report is written to investigate
the reproducibility of the submitted paper On the regularization of Wasserstein
GANs (2018). Second, among the experiments performed in the submitted paper,
five aspects were emphasized and reproduced: learning speed, stability,
robustness against hyperparameter, estimating the Wasserstein distance, and
various sampling method. Finally, we identify which parts of the contribution
can be reproduced, and at what cost in terms of resources. All source code for
reproduction is open to the public.
Rewrite this for me: This report investigates the reproducibility of the 2018 paper “On the regularization of Wasserstein GANs.” We focus on reproducing five key experimental aspects: learning speed, stability, hyperparameter robustness, Wasserstein distance estimation, and sampling methods. Our analysis identifies which contributions can be reliably reproduced and details the required computational resources. All source code for this reproduction study is publicly available.

input:
Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) were originally motivated (Kingma & Welling,
2014) as probabilistic generative models in which one performs approximate
Bayesian inference. The proposal of $\beta$-VAEs (Higgins et al., 2017) breaks
this interpretation and generalizes VAEs to application domains beyond
generative modeling (e.g., representation learning, clustering, or lossy data
compression) by introducing an objective function that allows practitioners to
trade off between the information content ("bit rate") of the latent
representation and the distortion of reconstructed data (Alemi et al., 2018).
In this paper, we reconsider this rate/distortion trade-off in the context of
hierarchical VAEs, i.e., VAEs with more than one layer of latent variables. We
identify a general class of inference models for which one can split the rate
into contributions from each layer, which can then be tuned independently. We
derive theoretical bounds on the performance of downstream tasks as functions
of the individual layers' rates and verify our theoretical findings in
large-scale experiments. Our results provide guidance for practitioners on
which region in rate-space to target for a given application.
Rewrite this for me:
Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) were initially conceived as probabilistic generative models for approximate Bayesian inference (Kingma & Welling, 2014). The development of $\beta$-VAEs (Higgins et al., 2017) later broadened their scope beyond pure generation. By introducing an objective that balances the informational "bit rate" of the latent code against the "distortion" in reconstruction, $\beta$-VAEs enabled applications in representation learning, clustering, and data compression (Alemi et al., 2018).

This paper re-examines this rate/distortion trade-off for hierarchical VAEs, which possess multiple latent layers. We define a general class of inference models where the total rate can be decomposed into separate contributions from each layer, allowing for their independent adjustment. We establish theoretical bounds on downstream task performance as functions of these individual layer rates, which we confirm through large-scale experiments. Our findings offer practical guidance on selecting optimal rate configurations for specific applications.

input:
Methods that learn representations of nodes in a graph play a critical role
in network analysis since they enable many downstream learning tasks. We
propose Graph2Gauss - an approach that can efficiently learn versatile node
embeddings on large scale (attributed) graphs that show strong performance on
tasks such as link prediction and node classification. Unlike most approaches
that represent nodes as point vectors in a low-dimensional continuous space, we
embed each node as a Gaussian distribution, allowing us to capture uncertainty
about the representation. Furthermore, we propose an unsupervised method that
handles inductive learning scenarios and is applicable to different types of
graphs: plain/attributed, directed/undirected. By leveraging both the network
structure and the associated node attributes, we are able to generalize to
unseen nodes without additional training. To learn the embeddings we adopt a
personalized ranking formulation w.r.t. the node distances that exploits the
natural ordering of the nodes imposed by the network structure. Experiments on
real world networks demonstrate the high performance of our approach,
outperforming state-of-the-art network embedding methods on several different
tasks. Additionally, we demonstrate the benefits of modeling uncertainty - by
analyzing it we can estimate neighborhood diversity and detect the intrinsic
latent dimensionality of a graph.
Rewrite this for me:
Methods for learning node representations are essential in network analysis, as they support a wide range of subsequent learning applications. We introduce Graph2Gauss, a scalable approach for learning versatile node embeddings on large (attributed) graphs, which delivers strong results in tasks like link prediction and node classification. Departing from standard methods that embed nodes as fixed point vectors in a low-dimensional space, we represent each node as a Gaussian distribution. This probabilistic formulation explicitly captures uncertainty in the representation.

Our method is unsupervised, supports inductive learning, and works across diverse graph types—plain or attributed, directed or undirected. It jointly leverages network structure and node attributes, enabling generalization to unseen nodes without retraining. The embeddings are learned through a personalized ranking objective based on node distances, which utilizes the natural ordering of nodes induced by the graph structure.

Experiments on real-world networks show that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art embedding techniques across multiple tasks. Moreover, the inherent modeling of uncertainty provides additional advantages: by analyzing it, we can estimate neighborhood diversity and infer the intrinsic latent dimensionality of a graph.

input:
This paper explores the use of self-ensembling for visual domain adaptation
problems. Our technique is derived from the mean teacher variant (Tarvainen et
al., 2017) of temporal ensembling (Laine et al;, 2017), a technique that
achieved state of the art results in the area of semi-supervised learning. We
introduce a number of modifications to their approach for challenging domain
adaptation scenarios and evaluate its effectiveness. Our approach achieves
state of the art results in a variety of benchmarks, including our winning
entry in the VISDA-2017 visual domain adaptation challenge. In small image
benchmarks, our algorithm not only outperforms prior art, but can also achieve
accuracy that is close to that of a classifier trained in a supervised fashion.
Rewrite this for me: This paper investigates the application of self-ensembling to visual domain adaptation. The method builds upon the mean teacher framework, an advanced form of temporal ensembling originally developed for semi-supervised learning. We adapt and enhance this approach to address the specific difficulties posed by domain adaptation. The resulting technique sets a new state of the art across multiple benchmarks, including our first-place entry in the VISDA-2017 challenge. Notably, on smaller image datasets, our method not only surpasses previous techniques but also approaches the accuracy of a fully supervised classifier.

input:
Most machine learning classifiers, including deep neural networks, are
vulnerable to adversarial examples. Such inputs are typically generated by
adding small but purposeful modifications that lead to incorrect outputs while
imperceptible to human eyes. The goal of this paper is not to introduce a
single method, but to make theoretical steps towards fully understanding
adversarial examples. By using concepts from topology, our theoretical analysis
brings forth the key reasons why an adversarial example can fool a classifier
($f_1$) and adds its oracle ($f_2$, like human eyes) in such analysis. By
investigating the topological relationship between two (pseudo)metric spaces
corresponding to predictor $f_1$ and oracle $f_2$, we develop necessary and
sufficient conditions that can determine if $f_1$ is always robust
(strong-robust) against adversarial examples according to $f_2$. Interestingly
our theorems indicate that just one unnecessary feature can make $f_1$ not
strong-robust, and the right feature representation learning is the key to
getting a classifier that is both accurate and strong-robust.
Rewrite this for me: Most machine learning classifiers, including deep neural networks, are susceptible to adversarial examples. These are inputs altered by small, deliberate perturbations that cause the model to err, yet remain indistinguishable from the original to a human observer. Rather than proposing a new defense technique, this paper aims to advance the theoretical foundation for comprehensively understanding such vulnerabilities. Employing topological concepts, our analysis uncovers the fundamental reasons a classifier (denoted \(f_1\)) can be fooled, while formally incorporating the perspective of an oracle (denoted \(f_2\), such as human perception). By examining the topological relationship between the pseudometric spaces of \(f_1\) and \(f_2\), we establish necessary and sufficient conditions to determine whether \(f_1\) is "strong-robust"—that is, consistently resilient to adversarial examples relative to \(f_2\). Notably, our theorems reveal that even one superfluous feature can break strong robustness. Consequently, learning an optimal feature representation is essential for achieving classifiers that are both highly accurate and fundamentally robust.

input:
In this paper, we propose a new feature extraction technique for program
execution logs. First, we automatically extract complex patterns from a
program's behavior graph. Then, we embed these patterns into a continuous space
by training an autoencoder. We evaluate the proposed features on a real-world
malicious software detection task. We also find that the embedding space
captures interpretable structures in the space of pattern parts.
Rewrite this for me: This paper introduces a novel method for extracting features from program execution logs. It begins by automatically identifying complex patterns from a program's behavior graph. These patterns are then embedded into a continuous vector space using a trained autoencoder. Evaluated on a real-world malware detection task, the technique also demonstrates that its embedding space organizes pattern components into interpretable structures.

input:
We compared the efficiency of the FlyHash model, an insect-inspired sparse
neural network (Dasgupta et al., 2017), to similar but non-sparse models in an
embodied navigation task. This requires a model to control steering by
comparing current visual inputs to memories stored along a training route. We
concluded the FlyHash model is more efficient than others, especially in terms
of data encoding.
Rewrite this for me: We evaluated the insect-inspired FlyHash model (Dasgupta et al., 2017) against comparable non-sparse models in an embodied navigation task. The task required steering control by comparing current visual inputs to stored route memories. Our results show that the FlyHash model is more efficient, particularly in its data encoding.

input:
In peer review, reviewers are usually asked to provide scores for the papers.
The scores are then used by Area Chairs or Program Chairs in various ways in
the decision-making process. The scores are usually elicited in a quantized
form to accommodate the limited cognitive ability of humans to describe their
opinions in numerical values. It has been found that the quantized scores
suffer from a large number of ties, thereby leading to a significant loss of
information. To mitigate this issue, conferences have started to ask reviewers
to additionally provide a ranking of the papers they have reviewed. There are
however two key challenges. First, there is no standard procedure for using
this ranking information and Area Chairs may use it in different ways
(including simply ignoring them), thereby leading to arbitrariness in the
peer-review process. Second, there are no suitable interfaces for judicious use
of this data nor methods to incorporate it in existing workflows, thereby
leading to inefficiencies. We take a principled approach to integrate the
ranking information into the scores. The output of our method is an updated
score pertaining to each review that also incorporates the rankings. Our
approach addresses the two aforementioned challenges by: (i) ensuring that
rankings are incorporated into the updates scores in the same manner for all
papers, thereby mitigating arbitrariness, and (ii) allowing to seamlessly use
existing interfaces and workflows designed for scores. We empirically evaluate
our method on synthetic datasets as well as on peer reviews from the ICLR 2017
conference, and find that it reduces the error by approximately 30% as compared
to the best performing baseline on the ICLR 2017 data.
Rewrite this for me:
In peer review, reviewers are typically asked to assign scores to papers. These scores are subsequently used by Area Chairs or Program Chairs to inform their decisions. Because it is cognitively difficult for people to express nuanced opinions as precise numbers, scores are usually collected in a quantized form (e.g., on a scale of 1 to 5). However, this quantization creates many tied scores, resulting in a substantial loss of information.

To address this problem, many conferences now also ask reviewers to rank the papers they have reviewed. Yet, this practice introduces two major challenges. First, there is no standard procedure for using these rankings; different Area Chairs may employ them inconsistently or ignore them entirely, introducing arbitrariness into the decision-making process. Second, existing review interfaces and workflows are designed for scores, not rankings. There are no suitable tools to incorporate ranking data judiciously, leading to operational inefficiencies.

We propose a principled method to integrate ranking information directly into the scores. Our approach produces an updated score for each review that reflects both the original rating and the relative ranking. This addresses the two challenges directly: (i) it ensures rankings are incorporated uniformly for all papers, eliminating arbitrariness, and (ii) it allows the use of existing interfaces and workflows built for scores, enabling seamless adoption.

We evaluate our method empirically using synthetic datasets and real peer-review data from the ICLR 2017 conference. On the ICLR 2017 data, our approach reduces the error by approximately 30% compared to the best-performing baseline.

input:
Many recent studies have probed status bias in the peer-review process of
academic journals and conferences. In this article, we investigated the
association between author metadata and area chairs' final decisions
(Accept/Reject) using our compiled database of 5,313 borderline submissions to
the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) from 2017 to
2022. We carefully defined elements in a cause-and-effect analysis, including
the treatment and its timing, pre-treatment variables, potential outcomes and
causal null hypothesis of interest, all in the context of study units being
textual data and under Neyman and Rubin's potential outcomes (PO) framework. We
found some weak evidence that author metadata was associated with articles'
final decisions. We also found that, under an additional stability assumption,
borderline articles from high-ranking institutions (top-30% or top-20%) were
less favored by area chairs compared to their matched counterparts. The results
were consistent in two different matched designs (odds ratio = 0.82 [95% CI:
0.67 to 1.00] in a first design and 0.83 [95% CI: 0.64 to 1.07] in a
strengthened design). We discussed how to interpret these results in the
context of multiple interactions between a study unit and different agents
(reviewers and area chairs) in the peer-review system.
Rewrite this for me:
Recent research has examined status bias within academic peer review. This article investigates the link between author metadata—specifically institutional affiliation—and final acceptance decisions for borderline submissions. Using a compiled database of 5,313 borderline papers from the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) between 2017 and 2022, we conducted a cause-and-effect analysis under Neyman and Rubin’s potential outcomes framework. We carefully defined the treatment, its timing, pre-treatment variables, and the causal null hypothesis, treating each submission as a textual study unit.

Our analysis revealed weak evidence of an association between author metadata and final decisions. Furthermore, under an added stability assumption, we found that borderline papers from high-ranking institutions (top-30% or top-20%) were less favored by area chairs compared to matched counterparts from lower-ranked institutions. This result was consistent across two matched designs, with odds ratios of 0.82 [95% CI: 0.67 to 1.00] in the initial design and 0.83 [95% CI: 0.64 to 1.07] in a strengthened design. We discuss the interpretation of these findings, considering the multiple interactions each submission has with different agents (reviewers and area chairs) in the peer-review system.

input:
We present a variational approximation to the information bottleneck of
Tishby et al. (1999). This variational approach allows us to parameterize the
information bottleneck model using a neural network and leverage the
reparameterization trick for efficient training. We call this method "Deep
Variational Information Bottleneck", or Deep VIB. We show that models trained
with the VIB objective outperform those that are trained with other forms of
regularization, in terms of generalization performance and robustness to
adversarial attack.
Rewrite this for me: We introduce a variational approximation to the information bottleneck principle (Tishby et al., 1999). This method, which we term the Deep Variational Information Bottleneck (Deep VIB), uses a neural network to parameterize the model and enables efficient training via the reparameterization trick. We demonstrate that models optimized with the VIB objective achieve superior generalization and greater robustness to adversarial attacks compared to those using other regularization techniques.

input:
Attention networks have proven to be an effective approach for embedding
categorical inference within a deep neural network. However, for many tasks we
may want to model richer structural dependencies without abandoning end-to-end
training. In this work, we experiment with incorporating richer structural
distributions, encoded using graphical models, within deep networks. We show
that these structured attention networks are simple extensions of the basic
attention procedure, and that they allow for extending attention beyond the
standard soft-selection approach, such as attending to partial segmentations or
to subtrees. We experiment with two different classes of structured attention
networks: a linear-chain conditional random field and a graph-based parsing
model, and describe how these models can be practically implemented as neural
network layers. Experiments show that this approach is effective for
incorporating structural biases, and structured attention networks outperform
baseline attention models on a variety of synthetic and real tasks: tree
transduction, neural machine translation, question answering, and natural
language inference. We further find that models trained in this way learn
interesting unsupervised hidden representations that generalize simple
attention.
Rewrite this for me:
Attention networks effectively integrate categorical inference into deep neural networks. Yet, many tasks require richer structural dependencies while maintaining end-to-end trainability. This work explores the incorporation of such structural distributions, encoded via graphical models, within deep networks. We demonstrate that these structured attention networks are straightforward extensions of basic attention. They enable moving beyond simple soft selection, allowing models to attend to elements like partial segmentations or syntactic subtrees.

We experiment with two specific classes: a linear-chain conditional random field and a graph-based parsing model, detailing their practical implementation as neural network layers. Experiments confirm the method's effectiveness for introducing structural biases. Structured attention networks outperform standard attention baselines across diverse synthetic and real-world tasks, including tree transduction, neural machine translation, question answering, and natural language inference.

Furthermore, models trained with this approach learn informative unsupervised hidden representations that generalize the capabilities of simple attention.

input:
We are proposing to use an ensemble of diverse specialists, where speciality
is defined according to the confusion matrix. Indeed, we observed that for
adversarial instances originating from a given class, labeling tend to be done
into a small subset of (incorrect) classes. Therefore, we argue that an
ensemble of specialists should be better able to identify and reject fooling
instances, with a high entropy (i.e., disagreement) over the decisions in the
presence of adversaries. Experimental results obtained confirm that
interpretation, opening a way to make the system more robust to adversarial
examples through a rejection mechanism, rather than trying to classify them
properly at any cost.
Rewrite this for me: We propose an ensemble of diverse specialists, with each specialist defined by patterns in the confusion matrix. Our observation shows that adversarial examples from a specific class are typically mislabeled into only a small, consistent set of incorrect classes. Consequently, we argue that a specialized ensemble can more effectively detect and reject these fooling instances. This is indicated by high entropy—or disagreement—among the specialists when facing adversaries. Our experimental results confirm this approach, demonstrating a path toward greater robustness via a rejection mechanism, rather than forcing correct classification at all costs.

input:
In this paper, we present Neural Phrase-based Machine Translation (NPMT). Our
method explicitly models the phrase structures in output sequences using
Sleep-WAke Networks (SWAN), a recently proposed segmentation-based sequence
modeling method. To mitigate the monotonic alignment requirement of SWAN, we
introduce a new layer to perform (soft) local reordering of input sequences.
Different from existing neural machine translation (NMT) approaches, NPMT does
not use attention-based decoding mechanisms. Instead, it directly outputs
phrases in a sequential order and can decode in linear time. Our experiments
show that NPMT achieves superior performances on IWSLT 2014
German-English/English-German and IWSLT 2015 English-Vietnamese machine
translation tasks compared with strong NMT baselines. We also observe that our
method produces meaningful phrases in output languages.
Rewrite this for me: This paper introduces Neural Phrase-based Machine Translation (NPMT). The approach explicitly models phrase structures in outputs using Sleep-Wake Networks (SWAN), a segmentation-based sequence model. To relax SWAN's monotonic alignment constraint, we add a new layer for (soft) local reordering of the input. Unlike standard neural machine translation (NMT), NPMT does not employ attention-based decoding. It sequentially generates complete phrases, enabling linear-time decoding. Experiments demonstrate that NPMT outperforms strong NMT baselines on IWSLT 2014 German-English/English-German and IWSLT 2015 English-Vietnamese tasks. Additionally, the model is shown to produce meaningful target-language phrases.

input:
We present LR-GAN: an adversarial image generation model which takes scene
structure and context into account. Unlike previous generative adversarial
networks (GANs), the proposed GAN learns to generate image background and
foregrounds separately and recursively, and stitch the foregrounds on the
background in a contextually relevant manner to produce a complete natural
image. For each foreground, the model learns to generate its appearance, shape
and pose. The whole model is unsupervised, and is trained in an end-to-end
manner with gradient descent methods. The experiments demonstrate that LR-GAN
can generate more natural images with objects that are more human recognizable
than DCGAN.
Rewrite this for me: We introduce LR-GAN, an adversarial model for image generation that explicitly incorporates scene structure and context. Departing from prior Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), our approach learns to recursively generate the image background and individual foreground elements. It then composes these parts by stitching each foreground onto the background in a contextually appropriate way to form a complete, natural image. For every foreground, the model learns to synthesize its appearance, shape, and pose. The entire system is unsupervised and trained end-to-end with gradient descent. Our experiments show that LR-GAN produces more natural images with more human-recognizable objects compared to the standard DCGAN.

input:
We describe a simple scheme that allows an agent to learn about its
environment in an unsupervised manner. Our scheme pits two versions of the same
agent, Alice and Bob, against one another. Alice proposes a task for Bob to
complete; and then Bob attempts to complete the task. In this work we will
focus on two kinds of environments: (nearly) reversible environments and
environments that can be reset. Alice will "propose" the task by doing a
sequence of actions and then Bob must undo or repeat them, respectively. Via an
appropriate reward structure, Alice and Bob automatically generate a curriculum
of exploration, enabling unsupervised training of the agent. When Bob is
deployed on an RL task within the environment, this unsupervised training
reduces the number of supervised episodes needed to learn, and in some cases
converges to a higher reward.
Rewrite this for me: We propose a simple, unsupervised method for an agent to learn about its environment. The approach involves two versions of the same agent, named Alice and Bob, which are set in opposition. Alice first proposes a task by performing a sequence of actions. Bob must then complete the task, which in this work involves either undoing Alice’s actions (in nearly reversible environments) or repeating them exactly (in environments that can be reset). Through a specific reward structure, this interaction causes Alice and Bob to automatically generate a progressive curriculum of exploration. When Bob is later deployed on a standard reinforcement learning task within that environment, this unsupervised pre-training reduces the number of supervised episodes required for learning and, in some cases, leads to convergence with a higher final reward.

input:
Maximum entropy modeling is a flexible and popular framework for formulating
statistical models given partial knowledge. In this paper, rather than the
traditional method of optimizing over the continuous density directly, we learn
a smooth and invertible transformation that maps a simple distribution to the
desired maximum entropy distribution. Doing so is nontrivial in that the
objective being maximized (entropy) is a function of the density itself. By
exploiting recent developments in normalizing flow networks, we cast the
maximum entropy problem into a finite-dimensional constrained optimization, and
solve the problem by combining stochastic optimization with the augmented
Lagrangian method. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of our
method, and applications to finance and computer vision show the flexibility
and accuracy of using maximum entropy flow networks.
Rewrite this for me: Maximum entropy modeling is a widely used framework for building statistical models from incomplete information. Traditionally, this involves directly optimizing a continuous density. In this work, we propose an alternative: we learn a smooth, invertible transformation that maps a simple base distribution to the target maximum entropy distribution. This approach is challenging because entropy is explicitly a function of the density. Leveraging advances in normalizing flows, we reformulate the maximum entropy problem as a finite-dimensional, constrained optimization. We solve it using stochastic optimization combined with the augmented Lagrangian method. Simulations confirm our method's efficacy, and applications in finance and computer vision highlight the flexibility and precision of these maximum entropy flow networks.

input:
With machine learning successfully applied to new daunting problems almost
every day, general AI starts looking like an attainable goal. However, most
current research focuses instead on important but narrow applications, such as
image classification or machine translation. We believe this to be largely due
to the lack of objective ways to measure progress towards broad machine
intelligence. In order to fill this gap, we propose here a set of concrete
desiderata for general AI, together with a platform to test machines on how
well they satisfy such desiderata, while keeping all further complexities to a
minimum.
Rewrite this for me: Machine learning now routinely tackles formidable challenges, making general artificial intelligence seem increasingly attainable. Yet, contemporary research remains largely concentrated on narrow domains like image classification. We argue this focus persists due to the absence of clear, objective benchmarks for measuring progress toward broad machine intelligence. To address this gap, we propose a set of concrete criteria for general AI, accompanied by a testing platform designed to evaluate machines against these standards while minimizing extraneous complexity.

input:
Neural networks that compute over graph structures are a natural fit for
problems in a variety of domains, including natural language (parse trees) and
cheminformatics (molecular graphs). However, since the computation graph has a
different shape and size for every input, such networks do not directly support
batched training or inference. They are also difficult to implement in popular
deep learning libraries, which are based on static data-flow graphs. We
introduce a technique called dynamic batching, which not only batches together
operations between different input graphs of dissimilar shape, but also between
different nodes within a single input graph. The technique allows us to create
static graphs, using popular libraries, that emulate dynamic computation graphs
of arbitrary shape and size. We further present a high-level library of
compositional blocks that simplifies the creation of dynamic graph models.
Using the library, we demonstrate concise and batch-wise parallel
implementations for a variety of models from the literature.
Rewrite this for me:
Neural networks designed for graph structures are inherently suited to fields like natural language processing (using parse trees) and cheminformatics (using molecular graphs). However, because each input graph has a unique size and shape, these networks cannot natively process data in batches for efficient training or inference. They are also challenging to build with standard deep learning libraries, which rely on static computational graphs.

We address this with a method called dynamic batching. It enables batching operations both across different input graphs and across nodes within a single graph. This approach allows us to use standard libraries to construct static graphs that mimic dynamic ones of any shape or size. We also introduce a high-level library of reusable components to simplify building dynamic graph models. With this library, we show how to implement various existing models concisely and in a fully parallel, batched manner.

input:
Although deep learning models have proven effective at solving problems in
natural language processing, the mechanism by which they come to their
conclusions is often unclear. As a result, these models are generally treated
as black boxes, yielding no insight of the underlying learned patterns. In this

Deep reinforcement learning has achieved many impressive results in recent

exploration and allowing to tackle sparse rewards in the downstream tasks. To

Deep generative models have achieved impressive success in recent years.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) continue to show outstanding performance in

from unfolding the RNN in time. We introduce the Skip RNN model which extends
existing RNN models by learning to skip state updates and shortens the
effective size of the computational graph. This model can also be encouraged to
perform fewer state updates through a budget constraint. We evaluate the
proposed model on various tasks and show how it can reduce the number of

performance of the baseline RNN models. Source code is publicly available at
https://imatge-upc.github.io/skiprnn-2017-telecombcn/ .

Motivated by the Stein's identity, our method extends the previous control

Skip connections made the training of very deep networks possible and have
become an indispensable component in a variety of neural architectures. A
completely satisfactory explanation for their success remains elusive. Here, we
present a novel explanation for the benefits of skip connections in training
very deep networks. The difficulty of training deep networks is partly due to
the singularities caused by the non-identifiability of the model. Several such
singularities have been identified in previous works: (i) overlap singularities
caused by the permutation symmetry of nodes in a given layer, (ii) elimination
singularities corresponding to the elimination, i.e. consistent deactivation,
of nodes, (iii) singularities generated by the linear dependence of the nodes.
These singularities cause degenerate manifolds in the loss landscape that slow
down learning. We argue that skip connections eliminate these singularities by
breaking the permutation symmetry of nodes, by reducing the possibility of node
elimination and by making the nodes less linearly dependent. Moreover, for
typical initializations, skip connections move the network away from the
"ghosts" of these singularities and sculpt the landscape around them to
alleviate the learning slow-down. These hypotheses are supported by evidence
from simplified models, as well as from experiments with deep networks trained
on real-world datasets.

Prior research has identified several such singularities: (i) *overlap singularities* stemming from the permutation symmetry of nodes within a layer; (ii) *elimination singularities*, which occur when nodes become consistently deactivated; and (iii) singularities caused by *linear dependence* among nodes. These create degenerate, flat regions in the loss landscape that impede learning.

We propose that skip connections mitigate this issue by directly addressing these singularities. They break the layer-wise permutation symmetry of nodes, decrease the likelihood of node elimination, and reduce linear dependencies between nodes. Furthermore, with standard parameter initializations, skip connections position the network away from the lingering influence, or "ghosts," of these singularities. They effectively reshape the loss landscape around these problematic areas to alleviate the characteristic slowdown in learning. Our hypotheses are corroborated by evidence from both simplified theoretical models and experiments with deep networks trained on real-world datasets.

In this work, we investigate Batch Normalization technique and propose its

It is widely believed that the success of deep convolutional networks is

with respect to the problem at hand. This is supported empirically by the

mapping that this loss of information is not a necessary condition to learn
representations that generalize well on complicated problems, such as ImageNet.
Via a cascade of homeomorphic layers, we build the i-RevNet, a network that can
be fully inverted up to the final projection onto the classes, i.e. no
information is discarded. Building an invertible architecture is difficult, for
one, because the local inversion is ill-conditioned, we overcome this by
providing an explicit inverse. An analysis of i-RevNets learned representations
suggests an alternative explanation for the success of deep networks by a
progressive contraction and linear separation with depth. To shed light on the
nature of the model learned by the i-RevNet we reconstruct linear
interpolations between natural image representations.

Analysis of the i-RevNet’s representations points to an alternative explanation for deep network success: a progressive contraction and linear separation of features with depth. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved impressive predictive performance
due to their ability to learn complex, non-linear relationships between

has led to DNNs being characterized as black boxes and consequently limited

hierarchical interpretations to explain DNN predictions through our proposed
method, agglomerative contextual decomposition (ACD). Given a prediction from a

along with the contribution of each cluster to the final prediction. This
hierarchy is optimized to identify clusters of features that the DNN learned
are predictive. Using examples from Stanford Sentiment Treebank and ImageNet,
we show that ACD is effective at diagnosing incorrect predictions and
identifying dataset bias. Through human experiments, we demonstrate that ACD
enables users both to identify the more accurate of two DNNs and to better

adversarial perturbations, implying that it captures fundamental aspects of the

In this work, we address the problem of musical timbre transfer, where the

Constant Q Transform (CQT) representation is particularly well-suited to

transferred the timbre while otherwise preserving the musical content, for both
monophonic and polyphonic samples.

Visual Question Answering (VQA) models have struggled with counting objects
in natural images so far. We identify a fundamental problem due to soft
attention in these models as a cause. To circumvent this problem, we propose a

Experiments on a toy task show the effectiveness of this component and we

We trace this issue to a core limitation of the soft attention mechanisms typically used. On the VQA v2 dataset, our single model achieves top results on number-based questions without harming performance in other categories, surpassing even ensemble methods. Furthermore, it delivers a 6.6% improvement on a challenging balanced metric for counting over a powerful baseline.

This paper introduces spectral normalization, a novel weight normalization method designed to stabilize the discriminator's training. The technique is computationally efficient and simple to integrate into existing models. Tests on CIFAR10, STL-10, and ILSVRC2012 datasets show that spectrally normalized GANs (SN-GANs) produce image quality that matches or surpasses results from prior stabilization approaches.

input:
Embedding graph nodes into a vector space can allow the use of machine
learning to e.g. predict node classes, but the study of node embedding
algorithms is immature compared to the natural language processing field
because of a diverse nature of graphs. We examine the performance of node
embedding algorithms with respect to graph centrality measures that
characterize diverse graphs, through systematic experiments with four node
embedding algorithms, four or five graph centralities, and six datasets.
Experimental results give insights into the properties of node embedding
algorithms, which can be a basis for further research on this topic.
Rewrite this for me: Mapping graph nodes into a vector space enables machine learning tasks like node classification. However, research into node embedding methods is less advanced than in fields like natural language processing, largely due to the inherent diversity of graph structures. This study systematically evaluates four embedding algorithms across six datasets, using four or five graph centrality measures to characterize different networks. The experimental results provide insights into the algorithms' properties, establishing a foundation for future research in this area.

input:
We introduce a new dataset of logical entailments for the purpose of
measuring models' ability to capture and exploit the structure of logical
expressions against an entailment prediction task. We use this task to compare
a series of architectures which are ubiquitous in the sequence-processing
literature, in addition to a new model class---PossibleWorldNets---which
computes entailment as a "convolution over possible worlds". Results show that
convolutional networks present the wrong inductive bias for this class of
problems relative to LSTM RNNs, tree-structured neural networks outperform LSTM
RNNs due to their enhanced ability to exploit the syntax of logic, and
PossibleWorldNets outperform all benchmarks.
Rewrite this for me: We present a novel dataset of logical entailments, designed to evaluate how well computational models can understand and utilize the structure of logical statements. Using this entailment prediction task, we compare several standard sequence-processing architectures and introduce a new model class—PossibleWorldNets—that determines entailment via a “convolution over possible worlds.” Our findings indicate that convolutional networks have an unsuitable inductive bias for such problems compared to LSTM RNNs. Furthermore, tree-structured networks surpass LSTMs by better leveraging logical syntax, while PossibleWorldNets exceed all other benchmarks.

input:
Neural network pruning techniques can reduce the parameter counts of trained
networks by over 90%, decreasing storage requirements and improving
computational performance of inference without compromising accuracy. However,
contemporary experience is that the sparse architectures produced by pruning
are difficult to train from the start, which would similarly improve training
performance.
  We find that a standard pruning technique naturally uncovers subnetworks
whose initializations made them capable of training effectively. Based on these
results, we articulate the "lottery ticket hypothesis:" dense,
randomly-initialized, feed-forward networks contain subnetworks ("winning
tickets") that - when trained in isolation - reach test accuracy comparable to
the original network in a similar number of iterations. The winning tickets we
find have won the initialization lottery: their connections have initial
weights that make training particularly effective.
  We present an algorithm to identify winning tickets and a series of
experiments that support the lottery ticket hypothesis and the importance of
these fortuitous initializations. We consistently find winning tickets that are
less than 10-20% of the size of several fully-connected and convolutional
feed-forward architectures for MNIST and CIFAR10. Above this size, the winning
tickets that we find learn faster than the original network and reach higher
test accuracy.
Rewrite this for me:
Neural network pruning can remove over 90% of a trained network's parameters, reducing storage needs and speeding up the process of running the model (inference) without losing accuracy. However, these sparse, pruned architectures have proven difficult to train successfully from scratch, which would similarly accelerate the training phase itself.

Our research reveals that a standard pruning method can inherently discover small subnetworks within a larger model that are capable of being trained effectively from the start. This leads us to propose the "lottery ticket hypothesis": within a dense, randomly-initialized neural network, there exist smaller subnetworks—"winning tickets"—that, when trained alone, can achieve test accuracy comparable to the original full network in a similar number of training steps. These subnetworks win a kind of "initialization lottery"; their initial weight values are fortuitously set in a way that makes them especially receptive to training.

We introduce an algorithm to find these winning tickets and provide extensive experimental evidence supporting the hypothesis. Across various standard architectures for MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets, we consistently identify winning tickets that contain less than 10-20% of the original network's parameters. Notably, when these subnetworks are slightly larger than this threshold, they not only learn faster than the original network but can also achieve higher final test accuracy.

input:
We characterize the singular values of the linear transformation associated
with a standard 2D multi-channel convolutional layer, enabling their efficient
computation. This characterization also leads to an algorithm for projecting a
convolutional layer onto an operator-norm ball. We show that this is an
effective regularizer; for example, it improves the test error of a deep
residual network using batch normalization on CIFAR-10 from 6.2\% to 5.3\%.
Rewrite this for me: We characterize the singular values of a standard 2D multi-channel convolutional layer, allowing for their efficient calculation. This result also provides an algorithm to project a convolutional layer onto an operator-norm ball. We demonstrate that this projection acts as an effective regularizer, improving a deep residual network's test error on CIFAR-10 from 6.2% to 5.3%.

input:
Understanding theoretical properties of deep and locally connected nonlinear
network, such as deep convolutional neural network (DCNN), is still a hard
problem despite its empirical success. In this paper, we propose a novel
theoretical framework for such networks with ReLU nonlinearity. The framework
explicitly formulates data distribution, favors disentangled representations
and is compatible with common regularization techniques such as Batch Norm. The
framework is built upon teacher-student setting, by expanding the student
forward/backward propagation onto the teacher's computational graph. The
resulting model does not impose unrealistic assumptions (e.g., Gaussian inputs,
independence of activation, etc). Our framework could help facilitate
theoretical analysis of many practical issues, e.g. overfitting,
generalization, disentangled representations in deep networks.
Rewrite this for me: Despite the empirical success of deep, locally connected networks like DCNNs, their theoretical properties remain difficult to understand. This paper introduces a new theoretical framework for such networks with ReLU activations. It explicitly models data distributions, promotes disentangled representations, and aligns with standard regularizers like Batch Norm. Built on a teacher-student setup, the framework expands the student’s forward and backward passes onto the teacher’s computational graph. Crucially, it avoids unrealistic assumptions such as Gaussian inputs or independent activations. This approach can enable clearer theoretical analysis of practical challenges, including overfitting, generalization, and feature disentanglement in deep networks.

input:
We present a Neural Program Search, an algorithm to generate programs from
natural language description and a small number of input/output examples. The
algorithm combines methods from Deep Learning and Program Synthesis fields by
designing rich domain-specific language (DSL) and defining efficient search
algorithm guided by a Seq2Tree model on it. To evaluate the quality of the
approach we also present a semi-synthetic dataset of descriptions with test
examples and corresponding programs. We show that our algorithm significantly
outperforms a sequence-to-sequence model with attention baseline.
Rewrite this for me: We introduce Neural Program Search, a method for generating programs from natural language descriptions and a few input/output examples. It merges deep learning with program synthesis by employing a specialized domain-specific language (DSL) and a search procedure directed by a Seq2Tree model. For evaluation, we provide a semi-synthetic dataset containing descriptions, test cases, and solution programs. Our results demonstrate that this approach substantially exceeds the performance of a standard sequence-to-sequence model with attention.

input:
Most state-of-the-art neural machine translation systems, despite being
different in architectural skeletons (e.g. recurrence, convolutional), share an
indispensable feature: the Attention. However, most existing attention methods
are token-based and ignore the importance of phrasal alignments, the key
ingredient for the success of phrase-based statistical machine translation. In
this paper, we propose novel phrase-based attention methods to model n-grams of
tokens as attention entities. We incorporate our phrase-based attentions into
the recently proposed Transformer network, and demonstrate that our approach
yields improvements of 1.3 BLEU for English-to-German and 0.5 BLEU for
German-to-English translation tasks on WMT newstest2014 using WMT'16 training
data.
Rewrite this for me: While state-of-the-art neural machine translation models vary in architecture, they all rely on attention mechanisms. Current methods, however, are typically token-based and overlook phrasal alignments—a cornerstone of traditional statistical approaches. This paper introduces novel phrase-based attention methods that model n-grams as fundamental units. We integrate these into the Transformer network, achieving improvements of 1.3 BLEU for English-to-German and 0.5 BLEU for German-to-English translation on the WMT newstest2014 benchmark, using WMT'16 training data.

input:
We introduce the problem of learning distributed representations of edits. By
combining a "neural editor" with an "edit encoder", our models learn to
represent the salient information of an edit and can be used to apply edits to
new inputs. We experiment on natural language and source code edit data. Our
evaluation yields promising results that suggest that our neural network models
learn to capture the structure and semantics of edits. We hope that this
interesting task and data source will inspire other researchers to work further
on this problem.
Rewrite this for me: We propose the task of learning distributed representations for edits. Our approach pairs a “neural editor” with an “edit encoder” to capture the essential information of an edit, enabling its application to new inputs. Evaluated on both natural language and source code edits, our models show promising results in learning the structural and semantic properties of edits. We present this as a compelling task and data source to encourage further research in this area.

input:
We propose a single neural probabilistic model based on variational
autoencoder that can be conditioned on an arbitrary subset of observed features
and then sample the remaining features in "one shot". The features may be both
real-valued and categorical. Training of the model is performed by stochastic
variational Bayes. The experimental evaluation on synthetic data, as well as
feature imputation and image inpainting problems, shows the effectiveness of
the proposed approach and diversity of the generated samples.
Rewrite this for me: We introduce a neural probabilistic model using a variational autoencoder. It can be conditioned on any subset of observed features—real-valued or categorical—and generate the remainder in a single step. Training relies on stochastic variational Bayes. Tests on synthetic data, feature imputation, and image inpainting demonstrate the method’s effectiveness and the diversity of its generated samples.

input:
Understanding and characterizing the subspaces of adversarial examples aid in
studying the robustness of deep neural networks (DNNs) to adversarial
perturbations. Very recently, Ma et al. (ICLR 2018) proposed to use local
intrinsic dimensionality (LID) in layer-wise hidden representations of DNNs to
study adversarial subspaces. It was demonstrated that LID can be used to
characterize the adversarial subspaces associated with different attack
methods, e.g., the Carlini and Wagner's (C&W) attack and the fast gradient sign
attack.
  In this paper, we use MNIST and CIFAR-10 to conduct two new sets of
experiments that are absent in existing LID analysis and report the limitation
of LID in characterizing the corresponding adversarial subspaces, which are (i)
oblivious attacks and LID analysis using adversarial examples with different
confidence levels; and (ii) black-box transfer attacks. For (i), we find that
the performance of LID is very sensitive to the confidence parameter deployed
by an attack, and the LID learned from ensembles of adversarial examples with
varying confidence levels surprisingly gives poor performance. For (ii), we
find that when adversarial examples are crafted from another DNN model, LID is
ineffective in characterizing their adversarial subspaces. These two findings
together suggest the limited capability of LID in characterizing the subspaces
of adversarial examples.
Rewrite this for me:
Understanding and characterizing the subspaces of adversarial examples helps in analyzing the robustness of deep neural networks (DNNs). Recently, Ma et al. (ICLR 2018) proposed using Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID) in the hidden layers of DNNs to study these adversarial subspaces. Their work showed that LID can characterize subspaces produced by specific attacks, such as the Carlini and Wagner (C&W) attack and the fast gradient sign method.

In this paper, we conduct two new sets of experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10, extending beyond prior LID analysis, and report limitations in its ability to characterize adversarial subspaces. The first experiment examines oblivious attacks and analyzes LID using adversarial examples generated with different confidence levels. We find that LID performance is highly sensitive to the attack’s confidence parameter, and that combining examples across confidence levels surprisingly yields poor results. The second experiment focuses on black-box transfer attacks, where adversarial examples are crafted from a separate DNN model. Here, LID proves ineffective in characterizing the resulting adversarial subspaces.

Together, these findings reveal significant constraints in LID’s capability to characterize the subspaces of adversarial examples, highlighting important practical limitations.

input:
Generative adversarial networks (GANs) form a generative modeling approach
known for producing appealing samples, but they are notably difficult to train.
One common way to tackle this issue has been to propose new formulations of the
GAN objective. Yet, surprisingly few studies have looked at optimization
methods designed for this adversarial training. In this work, we cast GAN
optimization problems in the general variational inequality framework. Tapping
into the mathematical programming literature, we counter some common
misconceptions about the difficulties of saddle point optimization and propose
to extend techniques designed for variational inequalities to the training of
GANs. We apply averaging, extrapolation and a computationally cheaper variant
that we call extrapolation from the past to the stochastic gradient method
(SGD) and Adam.
Rewrite this for me:
Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are a powerful generative modeling technique, celebrated for their ability to create high-quality samples. However, their training process is notoriously unstable. While much research has focused on developing new objective functions to address this, the optimization methods used for this adversarial training have received comparatively little attention.

In this work, we reframe GAN optimization within the general variational inequality framework. Drawing from established mathematical programming literature, we challenge certain misconceptions regarding saddle point optimization. We then propose adapting techniques specifically designed for variational inequalities—namely averaging, extrapolation, and a more efficient variant we term *extrapolation from the past*—to enhance standard optimizers like SGD and Adam for GAN training.

input:
Neural message passing algorithms for semi-supervised classification on
graphs have recently achieved great success. However, for classifying a node
these methods only consider nodes that are a few propagation steps away and the
size of this utilized neighborhood is hard to extend. In this paper, we use the
relationship between graph convolutional networks (GCN) and PageRank to derive
an improved propagation scheme based on personalized PageRank. We utilize this
propagation procedure to construct a simple model, personalized propagation of
neural predictions (PPNP), and its fast approximation, APPNP. Our model's
training time is on par or faster and its number of parameters on par or lower
than previous models. It leverages a large, adjustable neighborhood for
classification and can be easily combined with any neural network. We show that
this model outperforms several recently proposed methods for semi-supervised
classification in the most thorough study done so far for GCN-like models. Our
implementation is available online.
Rewrite this for me:
Neural message passing algorithms have recently delivered strong results in semi-supervised classification on graph-structured data. A key limitation, however, is that these methods typically rely on information from only a few nearby propagation steps, and expanding this receptive neighborhood is challenging.

In this work, we exploit the connection between graph convolutional networks (GCN) and PageRank to design a new propagation scheme based on personalized PageRank. We employ this procedure to build a straightforward model called PPNP (personalized propagation of neural predictions), along with its fast approximation, APPNP.

Our approach matches or surpasses prior models in training speed and parameter efficiency. Crucially, it can leverage a large, tunable neighborhood for classifying each node and integrates seamlessly with any underlying neural network. In the most comprehensive study of GCN-like models to date, we demonstrate that PPNP and APPNP outperform several recent methods for semi-supervised classification. Our implementation is publicly available.

input:
We identify obfuscated gradients, a kind of gradient masking, as a phenomenon
that leads to a false sense of security in defenses against adversarial
examples. While defenses that cause obfuscated gradients appear to defeat
iterative optimization-based attacks, we find defenses relying on this effect
can be circumvented. We describe characteristic behaviors of defenses
exhibiting the effect, and for each of the three types of obfuscated gradients
we discover, we develop attack techniques to overcome it. In a case study,
examining non-certified white-box-secure defenses at ICLR 2018, we find
obfuscated gradients are a common occurrence, with 7 of 9 defenses relying on
obfuscated gradients. Our new attacks successfully circumvent 6 completely, and
1 partially, in the original threat model each paper considers.
Rewrite this for me: We identify a phenomenon called obfuscated gradients—a form of gradient masking—that creates a false sense of security in defenses against adversarial examples. Although these defenses can appear robust by defeating iterative optimization-based attacks, we show they are ultimately circumventable. We outline the characteristic behaviors of such defenses and, for each of the three types of obfuscated gradients we uncover, we design specific attack techniques to defeat them. In a case study of non-certified white-box-secure defenses from ICLR 2018, we find obfuscated gradients are widespread: 7 out of 9 defenses rely on this effect. Our new attacks completely break 6 of these defenses and partially break 1, all within the original threat models assumed by the papers.

input:
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become the method of choice for
learning problems involving 2D planar images. However, a number of problems of
recent interest have created a demand for models that can analyze spherical
images. Examples include omnidirectional vision for drones, robots, and
autonomous cars, molecular regression problems, and global weather and climate
modelling. A naive application of convolutional networks to a planar projection
of the spherical signal is destined to fail, because the space-varying
distortions introduced by such a projection will make translational weight
sharing ineffective.
  In this paper we introduce the building blocks for constructing spherical
CNNs. We propose a definition for the spherical cross-correlation that is both
expressive and rotation-equivariant. The spherical correlation satisfies a
generalized Fourier theorem, which allows us to compute it efficiently using a
generalized (non-commutative) Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm. We
demonstrate the computational efficiency, numerical accuracy, and effectiveness
of spherical CNNs applied to 3D model recognition and atomization energy
regression.
Rewrite this for me:
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are the standard for processing conventional 2D images. Yet, emerging challenges increasingly require the analysis of data on a sphere, such as omnidirectional imagery for robotics and autonomous vehicles, molecular property prediction, and global climate modeling. Simply applying standard CNNs to a flattened projection of spherical data is inherently flawed, as the resulting spatial distortions undermine the fundamental translational weight-sharing principle of planar convolutions.

This paper presents the essential components for building CNNs directly on the sphere. We define a spherical cross-correlation operation that is both highly expressive and equivariant to 3D rotations. This correlation adheres to a generalized Fourier theorem, enabling its efficient computation via a non-commutative Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm. We validate our approach by demonstrating the computational efficiency, numerical accuracy, and practical performance of spherical CNNs on benchmark tasks, including 3D shape recognition and molecular energy regression.

input:
The inclusion of Computer Vision and Deep Learning technologies in
Agriculture aims to increase the harvest quality, and productivity of farmers.
During postharvest, the export market and quality evaluation are affected by
assorting of fruits and vegetables. In particular, apples are susceptible to a
wide range of defects that can occur during harvesting or/and during the
post-harvesting period. This paper aims to help farmers with post-harvest
handling by exploring if recent computer vision and deep learning methods such
as the YOLOv3 (Redmon & Farhadi (2018)) can help in detecting healthy apples
from apples with defects.
Rewrite this for me:
Computer Vision and Deep Learning are being applied in agriculture to enhance crop quality and farmer productivity. A key postharvest challenge is the sorting of fruits and vegetables, which directly impacts quality evaluation and export markets. Apples are especially prone to various defects arising during or after harvest. This paper investigates whether modern computer vision techniques, specifically the YOLOv3 model (Redmon & Farhadi, 2018), can effectively distinguish between healthy and defective apples to aid farmers in postharvest handling.

In this work, we analyze the reinstatement mechanism introduced by Ritter et
al. (2018) to reveal two classes of neurons that emerge in the agent's working
memory (an epLSTM cell) when trained using episodic meta-RL on an episodic
variant of the Harlow visual fixation task. Specifically, Abstract neurons
encode knowledge shared across tasks, while Episodic neurons carry information
relevant for a specific episode's task.

When an agent is trained via episodic meta-RL on an episodic Harlow task, two distinct neuron classes emerge in its working memory (an epLSTM). Abstract neurons encode knowledge common to all tasks, whereas Episodic neurons hold information specific to a single episode's objective.

The rate-distortion-perception function (RDPF; Blau and Michaeli, 2019) has
emerged as a useful tool for thinking about realism and distortion of
reconstructions in lossy compression. Unlike the rate-distortion function,
however, it is unknown whether encoders and decoders exist that achieve the
rate suggested by the RDPF. Building on results by Li and El Gamal (2018), we
show that the RDPF can indeed be achieved using stochastic, variable-length
codes. For this class of codes, we also prove that the RDPF lower-bounds the
achievable rate
Rewrite this for me:

However, unlike the classic rate-distortion function, it has been unclear whether practical encoders and decoders can achieve the rates it suggests. We demonstrate, by extending results from Li and El Gamal (2018), that the RDPF is indeed achievable using stochastic, variable-length codes. For this class of codes, we also prove that the RDPF provides a lower bound on any achievable rate.

input:
It is by now well-known that small adversarial perturbations can induce
classification errors in deep neural networks (DNNs). In this paper, we make
the case that sparse representations of the input data are a crucial tool for
combating such attacks. For linear classifiers, we show that a sparsifying
front end is provably effective against $\ell_{\infty}$-bounded attacks,
reducing output distortion due to the attack by a factor of roughly $K / N$
where $N$ is the data dimension and $K$ is the sparsity level. We then extend
this concept to DNNs, showing that a "locally linear" model can be used to
develop a theoretical foundation for crafting attacks and defenses.
Experimental results for the MNIST dataset show the efficacy of the proposed
sparsifying front end.
Rewrite this for me:
It is widely recognized that small, carefully crafted adversarial perturbations can cause deep neural networks (DNNs) to misclassify inputs. This paper argues that sparse representations of data are a vital defense mechanism against such attacks. For linear classifiers, we prove that a sparsifying front end robustly counters ℓ∞-bounded attacks, diminishing the attack’s output distortion by approximately a factor of *K*/*N*—where *N* is the data dimension and *K* is the sparsity. We generalize this principle to DNNs using a locally linear model, which provides a theoretical framework for designing both attacks and defenses. Experiments on MNIST confirm the effectiveness of the proposed sparsifying front end.

input:
We propose a new sample-efficient methodology, called Supervised Policy
Update (SPU), for deep reinforcement learning. Starting with data generated by
the current policy, SPU formulates and solves a constrained optimization
problem in the non-parameterized proximal policy space. Using supervised
regression, it then converts the optimal non-parameterized policy to a
parameterized policy, from which it draws new samples. The methodology is
general in that it applies to both discrete and continuous action spaces, and
can handle a wide variety of proximity constraints for the non-parameterized
optimization problem. We show how the Natural Policy Gradient and Trust Region
Policy Optimization (NPG/TRPO) problems, and the Proximal Policy Optimization
(PPO) problem can be addressed by this methodology. The SPU implementation is
much simpler than TRPO. In terms of sample efficiency, our extensive
experiments show SPU outperforms TRPO in Mujoco simulated robotic tasks and
outperforms PPO in Atari video game tasks.
Rewrite this for me:
We introduce a novel, sample-efficient approach for deep reinforcement learning named the Supervised Policy Update (SPU). The method begins with data from the current policy. SPU first defines and solves a constrained optimization within a non-parameterized proximal policy space. Subsequently, it employs supervised regression to transform this optimal solution into a parameterized policy, which is then used for sampling new data. This framework is general, applicable to both discrete and continuous actions, and accommodates a broad range of proximity constraints for its core optimization.

We demonstrate that SPU can effectively address the problems posed by Natural Policy Gradient/Trust Region Policy Optimization (NPG/TRPO) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Its implementation is notably simpler than TRPO. In extensive testing, SPU exhibits superior sample efficiency, outperforming TRPO on Mujoco robotic simulations and exceeding PPO's performance on Atari game tasks.

input:
We present a parameterized synthetic dataset called Moving Symbols to support
the objective study of video prediction networks. Using several instantiations
of the dataset in which variation is explicitly controlled, we highlight issues
in an existing state-of-the-art approach and propose the use of a performance
metric with greater semantic meaning to improve experimental interpretability.
Our dataset provides canonical test cases that will help the community better
understand, and eventually improve, the representations learned by such
networks in the future. Code is available at
https://github.com/rszeto/moving-symbols .
Rewrite this for me: We introduce Moving Symbols, a parameterized synthetic dataset designed for the objective evaluation of video prediction networks. By creating controlled variations within the dataset, we identify limitations in a current state-of-the-art method. We also advocate for a more semantically meaningful performance metric to enhance experimental clarity. This dataset offers canonical tests to help the community better understand and improve the internal representations learned by these models. Code is available at https://github.com/rszeto/moving-symbols.

input:
This work is a part of ICLR Reproducibility Challenge 2019, we try to
reproduce the results in the conference submission PADAM: Closing The
Generalization Gap of Adaptive Gradient Methods In Training Deep Neural
Networks. Adaptive gradient methods proposed in past demonstrate a degraded
generalization performance than the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with
momentum. The authors try to address this problem by designing a new
optimization algorithm that bridges the gap between the space of Adaptive
Gradient algorithms and SGD with momentum. With this method a new tunable
hyperparameter called partially adaptive parameter p is introduced that varies
between [0, 0.5]. We build the proposed optimizer and use it to mirror the
experiments performed by the authors. We review and comment on the empirical
analysis performed by the authors. Finally, we also propose a future direction
for further study of Padam. Our code is available at:
https://github.com/yashkant/Padam-Tensorflow
Rewrite this for me:
This study was conducted as part of the ICLR Reproducibility Challenge 2019. Our objective was to reproduce the findings presented in the conference submission “PADAM: Closing The Generalization Gap of Adaptive Gradient Methods In Training Deep Neural Networks.” Prior adaptive gradient methods have often shown inferior generalization performance compared to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with momentum. The paper’s authors address this issue by introducing a new optimizer designed to bridge the gap between adaptive methods and SGD. Their approach incorporates a tunable hyperparameter, the partially adaptive parameter *p*, which operates within the range [0, 0.5].

We implemented the proposed Padam optimizer and replicated the authors’ core experiments. This report reviews and provides commentary on their empirical analysis. Additionally, we suggest a potential direction for future research on the Padam method. Our reproduction code is publicly available at: https://github.com/yashkant/Padam-Tensorflow.

input:
We present a large-scale empirical study of catastrophic forgetting (CF) in
modern Deep Neural Network (DNN) models that perform sequential (or:
incremental) learning. A new experimental protocol is proposed that enforces
typical constraints encountered in application scenarios. As the investigation
is empirical, we evaluate CF behavior on the hitherto largest number of visual
classification datasets, from each of which we construct a representative
number of Sequential Learning Tasks (SLTs) in close alignment to previous works
on CF. Our results clearly indicate that there is no model that avoids CF for
all investigated datasets and SLTs under application conditions. We conclude
with a discussion of potential solutions and workarounds to CF, notably for the
EWC and IMM models.
Rewrite this for me:
We conduct a large-scale empirical investigation of catastrophic forgetting (CF) in modern Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) engaged in sequential learning. A novel experimental protocol is introduced, designed to reflect the typical constraints of real-world applications. This empirical study evaluates CF across the largest collection of visual classification datasets to date, generating a representative set of Sequential Learning Tasks (SLTs) consistent with prior CF research. Our findings demonstrate conclusively that no examined model successfully avoids CF across all datasets and SLTs under these practical conditions. The discussion concludes by exploring potential solutions and workarounds for CF, with particular attention given to the EWC and IMM models.
