input:
Deep learning models for graphs have advanced the state of the art on many
tasks. Despite their recent success, little is known about their robustness. We
investigate training time attacks on graph neural networks for node
classification that perturb the discrete graph structure. Our core principle is
to use meta-gradients to solve the bilevel problem underlying training-time
attacks, essentially treating the graph as a hyperparameter to optimize. Our
experiments show that small graph perturbations consistently lead to a strong
decrease in performance for graph convolutional networks, and even transfer to
unsupervised embeddings. Remarkably, the perturbations created by our algorithm
can misguide the graph neural networks such that they perform worse than a
simple baseline that ignores all relational information. Our attacks do not
assume any knowledge about or access to the target classifiers.
Rewrite this for me: Recent advances in graph neural networks have significantly improved performance on numerous tasks. However, their vulnerability to adversarial manipulation remains largely unexplored. This work examines training-time attacks that target node classification by altering the discrete structure of the graph. Our central approach employs meta-gradients to address the underlying bilevel optimization problem, effectively treating the graph itself as a learnable hyperparameter. Experiments demonstrate that even minor structural perturbations can cause substantial performance degradation in graph convolutional networks, with effects transferring to unsupervised embeddings. Notably, our method can mislead these models to underperform a simple baseline that disregards all relational information. These attacks require no prior knowledge of or access to the target classifiers.

input:
Multi-domain learning (MDL) aims at obtaining a model with minimal average
risk across multiple domains. Our empirical motivation is automated microscopy
data, where cultured cells are imaged after being exposed to known and unknown
chemical perturbations, and each dataset displays significant experimental
bias. This paper presents a multi-domain adversarial learning approach, MuLANN,
to leverage multiple datasets with overlapping but distinct class sets, in a
semi-supervised setting. Our contributions include: i) a bound on the average-
and worst-domain risk in MDL, obtained using the H-divergence; ii) a new loss
to accommodate semi-supervised multi-domain learning and domain adaptation;
iii) the experimental validation of the approach, improving on the state of the
art on two standard image benchmarks, and a novel bioimage dataset, Cell.
Rewrite this for me: Multi-domain learning (MDL) seeks a model that minimizes the average risk across several domains. Our work is empirically driven by automated microscopy data, where images of chemically perturbed cells exhibit strong experimental biases across different datasets. We propose a neural network for unsupervised anomaly detection with a novel
robust subspace recovery layer (RSR layer). This layer seeks to extract the
underlying subspace from a latent representation of the given data and removes
outliers that lie away from this subspace. It is used within an autoencoder.
The encoder maps the data into a latent space, from which the RSR layer
extracts the subspace. The decoder then smoothly maps back the underlying
subspace to a "manifold" close to the original inliers. Inliers and outliers
are distinguished according to the distances between the original and mapped
positions (small for inliers and large for outliers). Extensive numerical
experiments with both image and document datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art
precision and recall.

Anomalies are identified by measuring the reconstruction distance—small for inliers, large for outliers. Extensive tests on image and document datasets show state-of-the-art precision and recall.

We propose a novel node embedding of directed graphs to statistical
manifolds, which is based on a global minimization of pairwise relative entropy
and graph geodesics in a non-linear way. Each node is encoded with a
probability density function over a measurable space. Furthermore, we analyze
the connection between the geometrical properties of such embedding and their
efficient learning procedure. Extensive experiments show that our proposed
embedding is better in preserving the global geodesic information of graphs, as
well as outperforming existing embedding models on directed graphs in a variety
of evaluation metrics, in an unsupervised setting.

This approach encodes each node as a probability density function and achieves a non-linear, global minimization of pairwise relative entropy along graph geodesics. We examine the relationship between the geometric properties of this embedding and its efficient learning process. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our model better preserves global geodesic information and outperforms existing unsupervised embeddings for directed graphs across multiple evaluation metrics.

input:
The impressive lifelong learning in animal brains is primarily enabled by
plastic changes in synaptic connectivity. Importantly, these changes are not
passive, but are actively controlled by neuromodulation, which is itself under
the control of the brain. The resulting self-modifying abilities of the brain
play an important role in learning and adaptation, and are a major basis for
biological reinforcement learning. Here we show for the first time that
artificial neural networks with such neuromodulated plasticity can be trained
with gradient descent. Extending previous work on differentiable Hebbian
plasticity, we propose a differentiable formulation for the neuromodulation of
plasticity. We show that neuromodulated plasticity improves the performance of
neural networks on both reinforcement learning and supervised learning tasks.
In one task, neuromodulated plastic LSTMs with millions of parameters
outperform standard LSTMs on a benchmark language modeling task (controlling
for the number of parameters). We conclude that differentiable neuromodulation
of plasticity offers a powerful new framework for training neural networks.

Animal brains achieve their remarkable lifelong learning through plastic changes in synaptic connections. Crucially, these changes are not passive; they are actively regulated by neuromodulation, which is itself directed by the brain. We demonstrate, for the first time, that artificial neural networks featuring this same principle—neuromodulated plasticity—can be successfully trained using gradient descent. Building on prior research into differentiable Hebbian plasticity, we introduce a differentiable formulation for neuromodulating plasticity itself.

Our results show that neuromodulated plasticity enhances network performance in both reinforcement and supervised learning. In one benchmark language modeling task, neuromodulated plastic LSTMs with millions of parameters outperformed standard LSTMs of comparable size. We conclude that differentiable neuromodulation of plasticity provides a powerful and novel framework for training neural networks.

Euclidean geometry has historically been the typical "workhorse" for machine
learning applications due to its power and simplicity. However, it has recently
been shown that geometric spaces with constant non-zero curvature improve
representations and performance on a variety of data types and downstream
tasks. Consequently, generative models like Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
have been successfully generalized to elliptical and hyperbolic latent spaces.
While these approaches work well on data with particular kinds of biases e.g.
tree-like data for a hyperbolic VAE, there exists no generic approach unifying
and leveraging all three models. We develop a Mixed-curvature Variational
Autoencoder, an efficient way to train a VAE whose latent space is a product of
constant curvature Riemannian manifolds, where the per-component curvature is
fixed or learnable. This generalizes the Euclidean VAE to curved latent spaces
and recovers it when curvatures of all latent space components go to 0.

To address this, we introduce the Mixed-curvature Variational Autoencoder. This model provides an efficient method for training a VAE whose latent space is a product of constant-curvature Riemannian manifolds, with each component's curvature being either fixed or learnable. This approach generalizes the Euclidean VAE to curved settings and naturally recovers it when all curvatures approach zero.

input:
We explore various methods for computing sentence representations from
pre-trained word embeddings without any training, i.e., using nothing but
random parameterizations. Our aim is to put sentence embeddings on more solid
footing by 1) looking at how much modern sentence embeddings gain over random
methods---as it turns out, surprisingly little; and by 2) providing the field
with more appropriate baselines going forward---which are, as it turns out,
quite strong. We also make important observations about proper experimental
protocol for sentence classification evaluation, together with recommendations
for future research.

Our goal is to establish a more rigorous foundation for sentence embeddings by demonstrating two key points: first, that current advanced methods show surprisingly minimal gains over these random baselines; and second, by providing the research community with stronger, more appropriate baseline models for future work. We also outline crucial experimental guidelines and recommendations for sentence classification evaluation.

input:
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are one of the most popular tools for
learning complex high dimensional distributions. However, generalization
properties of GANs have not been well understood. In this paper, we analyze the
generalization of GANs in practical settings. We show that discriminators
trained on discrete datasets with the original GAN loss have poor
generalization capability and do not approximate the theoretically optimal
discriminator. We propose a zero-centered gradient penalty for improving the
generalization of the discriminator by pushing it toward the optimal
discriminator. The penalty guarantees the generalization and convergence of
GANs. Experiments on synthetic and large scale datasets verify our theoretical
analysis.
Rewrite this for me: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are a leading method for learning complex data distributions, yet their generalization behavior remains poorly understood. This paper analyzes GAN generalization in practical scenarios. We demonstrate that discriminators trained on discrete data with the standard GAN loss generalize poorly and deviate from the theoretically optimal discriminator. To address this, we introduce a zero-centered gradient penalty. This penalty enhances the discriminator's generalization by steering it toward the optimal function, thereby guaranteeing both generalization and convergence. Our theoretical findings are validated through experiments on synthetic and large-scale datasets.

input:
In this paper we propose to perform model ensembling in a multiclass or a
multilabel learning setting using Wasserstein (W.) barycenters. Optimal
transport metrics, such as the Wasserstein distance, allow incorporating
semantic side information such as word embeddings. Using W. barycenters to find
the consensus between models allows us to balance confidence and semantics in
finding the agreement between the models. We show applications of Wasserstein
ensembling in attribute-based classification, multilabel learning and image
captioning generation. These results show that the W. ensembling is a viable
alternative to the basic geometric or arithmetic mean ensembling.
Rewrite this for me: This paper introduces a method for model ensembling in multiclass and multilabel learning using Wasserstein barycenters. Optimal transport metrics, like the Wasserstein distance, enable the integration of semantic side information, such as word embeddings. Employing Wasserstein barycenters to establish consensus among models effectively balances confidence and semantic meaning. We demonstrate applications in attribute-based classification, multilabel learning, and image captioning. The results confirm that Wasserstein ensembling is a viable alternative to traditional geometric or arithmetic mean approaches.

input:
We present a method that learns to integrate temporal information, from a
learned dynamics model, with ambiguous visual information, from a learned
vision model, in the context of interacting agents. Our method is based on a
graph-structured variational recurrent neural network (Graph-VRNN), which is
trained end-to-end to infer the current state of the (partially observed)
world, as well as to forecast future states. We show that our method
outperforms various baselines on two sports datasets, one based on real
basketball trajectories, and one generated by a soccer game engine.
Rewrite this for me: Our approach learns to combine uncertain visual data from a vision model with temporal dynamics from a learned model, focusing on multi-agent interactions. It employs a graph-structured variational recurrent neural network (Graph-VRNN), trained end-to-end to infer the current, partially-observed state and to predict future states. We demonstrate that this method surpasses several baseline models on two sports datasets: one containing real basketball trajectories and another generated by a soccer game engine.

input:
Modern neural networks are over-parametrized. In particular, each rectified
linear hidden unit can be modified by a multiplicative factor by adjusting
input and output weights, without changing the rest of the network. Inspired by
the Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm, we introduce a fast iterative method for
minimizing the L2 norm of the weights, equivalently the weight decay
regularizer. It provably converges to a unique solution. Interleaving our
algorithm with SGD during training improves the test accuracy. For small
batches, our approach offers an alternative to batch-and group-normalization on
CIFAR-10 and ImageNet with a ResNet-18.
Rewrite this for me: Modern neural networks are over-parametrized. For instance, a ReLU unit’s influence can be scaled by adjusting its incoming and outgoing weights without altering the rest of the network. Taking inspiration from the Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm, we propose a fast, iterative method to minimize the L2 norm of the weights—equivalent to applying weight decay. The algorithm provably converges to a unique solution. When interleaved with SGD, it improves test accuracy. For small batches, our method provides an effective alternative to batch and group normalization on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet using a ResNet-18.

input:
We present graph wavelet neural network (GWNN), a novel graph convolutional
neural network (CNN), leveraging graph wavelet transform to address the
shortcomings of previous spectral graph CNN methods that depend on graph
Fourier transform. Different from graph Fourier transform, graph wavelet
transform can be obtained via a fast algorithm without requiring matrix
eigendecomposition with high computational cost. Moreover, graph wavelets are
sparse and localized in vertex domain, offering high efficiency and good
interpretability for graph convolution. The proposed GWNN significantly
outperforms previous spectral graph CNNs in the task of graph-based
semi-supervised classification on three benchmark datasets: Cora, Citeseer and
Pubmed.
Rewrite this for me: We introduce the graph wavelet neural network (GWNN), a new graph convolutional neural network. It uses graph wavelet transform to overcome the limitations of earlier spectral methods based on graph Fourier transform. Unlike the Fourier approach, the wavelet transform can be computed quickly without expensive matrix eigendecomposition. Graph wavelets are also sparse and localized in the vertex domain, making graph convolution more efficient and interpretable. Our GWNN substantially outperforms previous spectral graph CNNs in semi-supervised classification tasks on the Cora, Citeseer, and Pubmed benchmark datasets.

input:
We present the perceptor gradients algorithm -- a novel approach to learning
symbolic representations based on the idea of decomposing an agent's policy
into i) a perceptor network extracting symbols from raw observation data and
ii) a task encoding program which maps the input symbols to output actions. We
show that the proposed algorithm is able to learn representations that can be
directly fed into a Linear-Quadratic Regulator (LQR) or a general purpose A*
planner. Our experimental results confirm that the perceptor gradients
algorithm is able to efficiently learn transferable symbolic representations as
well as generate new observations according to a semantically meaningful
specification.
Rewrite this for me: We introduce the perceptor gradients algorithm, a novel method for learning symbolic representations. It decomposes an agent's policy into two components: a perceptor network that extracts symbols from raw observations, and a task program that maps these symbols to actions. We demonstrate that the algorithm learns representations directly compatible with a Linear-Quadratic Regulator (LQR) or a general A* planner. Experiments confirm that perceptor gradients efficiently learns transferable symbolic representations and can generate new observations based on semantically meaningful specifications.

input:
We study the robustness to symmetric label noise of GNNs training procedures.
By combining the nonlinear neural message-passing models (e.g. Graph
Isomorphism Networks, GraphSAGE, etc.) with loss correction methods, we present
a noise-tolerant approach for the graph classification task. Our experiments
show that test accuracy can be improved under the artificial symmetric noisy
setting.
Rewrite this for me: We examine the robustness of Graph Neural Network (GNN) training to symmetric label noise. By integrating nonlinear message-passing models with loss correction techniques, we propose a noise-tolerant method for graph classification. Experiments demonstrate improved test accuracy under artificially generated symmetric noise.

input:
The recent use of `Big Code' with state-of-the-art deep learning methods
offers promising avenues to ease program source code writing and correction. As
a first step towards automatic code repair, we implemented a graph neural
network model that predicts token types for Javascript programs. The
predictions achieve an accuracy above $90\%$, which improves on previous
similar work.
Rewrite this for me: Employing “Big Code” and advanced deep learning presents promising ways to simplify writing and correcting source code. As an initial step toward automatic repair, we built a graph neural network to predict token types in JavaScript. Its predictions exceed 90% accuracy, improving upon prior similar efforts.

input:
In this paper we consider self-supervised representation learning to improve
sample efficiency in reinforcement learning (RL). We propose a forward
prediction objective for simultaneously learning embeddings of states and
action sequences. These embeddings capture the structure of the environment's
dynamics, enabling efficient policy learning. We demonstrate that our action
embeddings alone improve the sample efficiency and peak performance of
model-free RL on control from low-dimensional states. By combining state and
action embeddings, we achieve efficient learning of high-quality policies on
goal-conditioned continuous control from pixel observations in only 1-2 million
environment steps.
Rewrite this for me: This paper explores self-supervised representation learning to enhance the sample efficiency of reinforcement learning (RL). We introduce a forward prediction objective that learns joint embeddings for states and action sequences. These embeddings encode the structure of the environment's dynamics, which facilitates efficient policy learning. Our results show that using the learned action embeddings alone boosts the sample efficiency and peak performance of model-free RL in low-dimensional state control. Furthermore, combining state and action embeddings enables efficient learning of high-quality, goal-conditioned policies from pixel observations in just 1-2 million environment steps.

input:
We study the problem of learning permutation invariant representations that
can capture "flexible" notions of containment. We formalize this problem via a
measure theoretic definition of multisets, and obtain a theoretically-motivated
learning model. We propose training this model on a novel task: predicting the
size of the symmetric difference (or intersection) between pairs of multisets.
We demonstrate that our model not only performs very well on predicting
containment relations (and more effectively predicts the sizes of symmetric
differences and intersections than DeepSets-based approaches with unconstrained
object representations), but that it also learns meaningful representations.
Rewrite this for me: This research addresses the problem of learning permutation-invariant representations capable of capturing flexible containment concepts. Using a measure-theoretic definition of multisets, we derive a theoretically-grounded learning model. We train this model on a novel objective: predicting the size of the symmetric difference or intersection between multiset pairs. Our model excels at predicting containment relations and outperforms DeepSets-based approaches in estimating symmetric difference and intersection sizes. Furthermore, it learns semantically meaningful representations.

input:
One way to interpret trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is by inspecting
characteristics that neurons in the model respond to, such as by iteratively
optimising the model input (e.g., an image) to maximally activate specific
neurons. However, this requires a careful selection of hyper-parameters to
generate interpretable examples for each neuron of interest, and current
methods rely on a manual, qualitative evaluation of each setting, which is
prohibitively slow. We introduce a new metric that uses Fr\'echet Inception
Distance (FID) to encourage similarity between model activations for real and
generated data. This provides an efficient way to evaluate a set of generated
examples for each setting of hyper-parameters. We also propose a novel
GAN-based method for generating explanations that enables an efficient search
through the input space and imposes a strong prior favouring realistic outputs.
We apply our approach to a classification model trained to predict whether a
music audio recording contains singing voice. Our results suggest that this
proposed metric successfully selects hyper-parameters leading to interpretable
examples, avoiding the need for manual evaluation. Moreover, we see that
examples synthesised to maximise or minimise the predicted probability of
singing voice presence exhibit vocal or non-vocal characteristics,
respectively, suggesting that our approach is able to generate suitable
explanations for understanding concepts learned by a neural network.
Rewrite this for me:
A key method for interpreting trained deep neural networks (DNNs) involves analyzing what activates specific neurons, often by optimizing an input—like an image—to maximally excite them. However, this process demands careful hyper-parameter tuning to produce clear, interpretable examples for each neuron. Current techniques rely on manual, qualitative assessment of every hyper-parameter setting, which is impractically slow.

To address this, we introduce a new metric based on the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) that promotes similarity between the model’s activations for real data and for generated examples. This offers an efficient, automated way to evaluate hyper-parameter sets. We also propose a novel GAN-based explanation method that enables efficient exploration of the input space while incorporating a strong prior toward realistic outputs.

We applied our approach to a classifier trained to detect singing voice in music audio. Results indicate that our metric successfully selects hyper-parameters yielding interpretable examples, eliminating the need for manual inspection. Furthermore, examples synthesized to either maximize or minimize the predicted probability of singing voice consistently exhibit vocal or non-vocal traits, respectively. This demonstrates that our method can generate meaningful explanations for understanding the concepts a neural network has learned.

input:
We propose Symplectic Recurrent Neural Networks (SRNNs) as learning
algorithms that capture the dynamics of physical systems from observed
trajectories. An SRNN models the Hamiltonian function of the system by a neural
network and furthermore leverages symplectic integration, multiple-step
training and initial state optimization to address the challenging numerical
issues associated with Hamiltonian systems. We show that SRNNs succeed reliably
on complex and noisy Hamiltonian systems. We also show how to augment the SRNN
integration scheme in order to handle stiff dynamical systems such as bouncing
billiards.
Rewrite this for me: Symplectic Recurrent Neural Networks (SRNNs) are designed to learn the dynamics of physical systems from observed data. They achieve this by using a neural network to model the system's Hamiltonian function. To address the numerical challenges inherent in Hamiltonian systems, SRNNs incorporate symplectic integration, multi-step training, and initial state optimization. These models reliably succeed on complex and noisy Hamiltonian systems. Furthermore, their integration scheme can be augmented to manage stiff dynamics, such as those in bouncing billiards.

input:
Spectral embedding is a popular technique for the representation of graph
data. Several regularization techniques have been proposed to improve the
quality of the embedding with respect to downstream tasks like clustering. In
this paper, we explain on a simple block model the impact of the complete graph
regularization, whereby a constant is added to all entries of the adjacency
matrix. Specifically, we show that the regularization forces the spectral
embedding to focus on the largest blocks, making the representation less
sensitive to noise or outliers. We illustrate these results on both on both
synthetic and real data, showing how regularization improves standard
clustering scores.
Rewrite this for me:
Spectral embedding is a common method for representing graph data. To enhance such embeddings for tasks like clustering, various regularization approaches exist. This paper analyzes the effect of one specific technique—complete graph regularization, which adds a constant to every entry of the adjacency matrix. Using a simple block model, we demonstrate that this regularization directs the spectral embedding to prioritize the largest blocks, thereby reducing its sensitivity to noise and outliers. We validate these findings on both synthetic and real-world data, where regularization consistently improves standard clustering performance.

input:
In this work we study locality and compositionality in the context of
learning representations for Zero Shot Learning (ZSL). In order to well-isolate
the importance of these properties in learned representations, we impose the
additional constraint that, differently from most recent work in ZSL, no
pre-training on different datasets (e.g. ImageNet) is performed. The results of
our experiments show how locality, in terms of small parts of the input, and
compositionality, i.e. how well can the learned representations be expressed as
a function of a smaller vocabulary, are both deeply related to generalization
and motivate the focus on more local-aware models in future research directions
for representation learning.
Rewrite this for me: This research examines the role of locality and compositionality within representation learning for Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL). To clearly isolate the impact of these properties, we adopt a strict constraint: unlike most contemporary ZSL methods, our models undergo no pre-training on external datasets like ImageNet. Our experimental findings demonstrate that both locality—focusing on small input parts—and compositionality—the ability to express representations with a compact vocabulary—are fundamentally linked to model generalization. These results strongly advocate for a greater emphasis on local-aware architectures in future representation learning research.

input:
We consider training machine learning models that are fair in the sense that
their performance is invariant under certain sensitive perturbations to the
inputs. For example, the performance of a resume screening system should be
invariant under changes to the gender and/or ethnicity of the applicant. We
formalize this notion of algorithmic fairness as a variant of individual
fairness and develop a distributionally robust optimization approach to enforce
it during training. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach on
two ML tasks that are susceptible to gender and racial biases.
Rewrite this for me: We propose training machine learning models to be fair by ensuring their performance remains stable when specific, sensitive attributes in the input data are altered. For instance, a model screening resumes should perform consistently regardless of changes to an applicant's gender or ethnicity. We define this fairness concept as a form of individual fairness and introduce a training method based on distributionally robust optimization to achieve it. Our approach is shown to effectively mitigate gender and racial biases in two susceptible machine learning tasks.

input:
Deep Reinforcement Learning (Deep RL) has been receiving increasingly more
attention thanks to its encouraging performance on a variety of control tasks.
Yet, conventional regularization techniques in training neural networks (e.g.,
$L_2$ regularization, dropout) have been largely ignored in RL methods,
possibly because agents are typically trained and evaluated in the same
environment, and because the deep RL community focuses more on high-level
algorithm designs. In this work, we present the first comprehensive study of
regularization techniques with multiple policy optimization algorithms on
continuous control tasks. Interestingly, we find conventional regularization
techniques on the policy networks can often bring large improvement, especially
on harder tasks. Our findings are shown to be robust against training
hyperparameter variations. We also compare these techniques with the more
widely used entropy regularization. In addition, we study regularizing
different components and find that only regularizing the policy network is
typically the best. We further analyze why regularization may help
generalization in RL from four perspectives - sample complexity, reward
distribution, weight norm, and noise robustness. We hope our study provides
guidance for future practices in regularizing policy optimization algorithms.
Our code is available at https://github.com/xuanlinli17/iclr2021_rlreg .
Rewrite this for me:
Deep Reinforcement Learning (Deep RL) has attracted growing attention due to its strong performance across numerous control tasks. However, standard neural network regularization methods—such as L₂ regularization and dropout—have seen limited adoption in RL. This may be because agents are usually trained and tested in identical environments, and because the field often prioritizes high-level algorithmic innovation.

In this paper, we conduct the first broad investigation of regularization techniques using multiple policy optimization algorithms on continuous control benchmarks. Notably, we demonstrate that applying conventional regularization to policy networks frequently yields significant gains, particularly on more difficult tasks. These results prove robust across variations in training hyperparameters.

We also compare these methods to the more common approach of entropy regularization. Furthermore, by regularizing different network components, we find that focusing solely on the policy network generally works best. To understand why regularization aids generalization in RL, we provide analysis from four angles: sample complexity, reward distribution, weight norms, and robustness to noise.

We hope this study offers practical guidance for integrating regularization into policy optimization. Our code is available at https://github.com/xuanlinli17/iclr2021_rlreg.

input:
We propose an algorithm combining calibrated prediction and generalization
bounds from learning theory to construct confidence sets for deep neural
networks with PAC guarantees---i.e., the confidence set for a given input
contains the true label with high probability. We demonstrate how our approach
can be used to construct PAC confidence sets on ResNet for ImageNet, a visual
object tracking model, and a dynamics model for the half-cheetah reinforcement
learning problem.
Rewrite this for me: We introduce an algorithm that merges calibrated prediction with learning-theoretic generalization bounds to build PAC-guaranteed confidence sets for deep neural networks. This ensures the set contains the true label with high probability. We validate our method by constructing such sets for a ResNet on ImageNet, a visual object tracker, and a dynamics model in a half-cheetah reinforcement learning task.

input:
We address the problem of graph classification based only on structural
information. Inspired by natural language processing techniques (NLP), our
model sequentially embeds information to estimate class membership
probabilities. Besides, we experiment with NLP-like variational regularization
techniques, making the model predict the next node in the sequence as it reads
it. We experimentally show that our model achieves state-of-the-art
classification results on several standard molecular datasets. Finally, we
perform a qualitative analysis and give some insights on whether the node
prediction helps the model better classify graphs.
Rewrite this for me: We tackle graph classification using only structural data. Drawing from natural language processing (NLP), our approach sequentially embeds information to estimate class probabilities. We also apply NLP-style variational regularization, training the model to predict the next node in a sequence as it processes the graph. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art classification performance on standard molecular datasets. A qualitative analysis then explores whether this node prediction task genuinely aids classification accuracy.

input:
In this paper, we introduce Symplectic ODE-Net (SymODEN), a deep learning
framework which can infer the dynamics of a physical system, given by an
ordinary differential equation (ODE), from observed state trajectories. To
achieve better generalization with fewer training samples, SymODEN incorporates
appropriate inductive bias by designing the associated computation graph in a
physics-informed manner. In particular, we enforce Hamiltonian dynamics with
control to learn the underlying dynamics in a transparent way, which can then
be leveraged to draw insight about relevant physical aspects of the system,
such as mass and potential energy. In addition, we propose a parametrization
which can enforce this Hamiltonian formalism even when the generalized
coordinate data is embedded in a high-dimensional space or we can only access
velocity data instead of generalized momentum. This framework, by offering
interpretable, physically-consistent models for physical systems, opens up new
possibilities for synthesizing model-based control strategies.
Rewrite this for me:
This paper presents Symplectic ODE-Net (SymODEN), a deep learning framework designed to infer the governing ordinary differential equations (ODEs) of a physical system from observed state trajectories. To enhance generalization with limited data, SymODEN incorporates physics-informed inductive bias by structuring its computation graph to respect Hamiltonian dynamics with control. This approach learns the underlying system dynamics in a transparent and interpretable manner, allowing for the extraction of physical insights, such as properties related to mass and potential energy.

Furthermore, we introduce a novel parametrization that ensures adherence to Hamiltonian structure even when generalized coordinates are embedded in high-dimensional spaces, or when only velocity data—rather than canonical momentum—is available. By generating interpretable and physically-consistent models, this framework enables new opportunities for developing model-based control strategies.

input:
Graph embedding techniques have been increasingly deployed in a multitude of
different applications that involve learning on non-Euclidean data. However,
existing graph embedding models either fail to incorporate node attribute
information during training or suffer from node attribute noise, which
compromises the accuracy. Moreover, very few of them scale to large graphs due
to their high computational complexity and memory usage. In this paper we
propose GraphZoom, a multi-level framework for improving both accuracy and
scalability of unsupervised graph embedding algorithms. GraphZoom first
performs graph fusion to generate a new graph that effectively encodes the
topology of the original graph and the node attribute information. This fused
graph is then repeatedly coarsened into much smaller graphs by merging nodes
with high spectral similarities. GraphZoom allows any existing embedding
methods to be applied to the coarsened graph, before it progressively refine
the embeddings obtained at the coarsest level to increasingly finer graphs. We
have evaluated our approach on a number of popular graph datasets for both
transductive and inductive tasks. Our experiments show that GraphZoom can
substantially increase the classification accuracy and significantly accelerate
the entire graph embedding process by up to 40.8x, when compared to the
state-of-the-art unsupervised embedding methods.
Rewrite this for me:
Graph embedding methods are widely used for learning from non-Euclidean data, yet current models face significant limitations. Many either neglect valuable node attribute information during training or are vulnerable to noise within those attributes, which reduces result accuracy. Furthermore, most techniques struggle with large-scale graphs due to high computational and memory demands.

To address these issues, we introduce GraphZoom, a multi-level framework designed to enhance both the accuracy and scalability of unsupervised graph embedding. GraphZoom begins with a graph fusion step, creating a new graph that integrates the original network topology with node attributes. This fused graph is then iteratively coarsened by merging spectrally similar nodes, producing progressively smaller approximations.

Any existing embedding method can be efficiently applied to the smallest, coarsened graph. GraphZoom then refines these coarse embeddings through a progressive refinement phase, lifting them back through the hierarchy of graphs to produce final, high-quality embeddings for the original network.

Evaluated on multiple benchmark datasets for transductive and inductive tasks, GraphZoom demonstrates substantial improvements. It not only boosts classification accuracy but also accelerates the embedding process by up to 40.8 times compared to state-of-the-art unsupervised methods.

input:
Distributed optimization is vital in solving large-scale machine learning
problems. A widely-shared feature of distributed optimization techniques is the
requirement that all nodes complete their assigned tasks in each computational
epoch before the system can proceed to the next epoch. In such settings, slow
nodes, called stragglers, can greatly slow progress. To mitigate the impact of
stragglers, we propose an online distributed optimization method called Anytime
Minibatch. In this approach, all nodes are given a fixed time to compute the
gradients of as many data samples as possible. The result is a variable
per-node minibatch size. Workers then get a fixed communication time to average
their minibatch gradients via several rounds of consensus, which are then used
to update primal variables via dual averaging. Anytime Minibatch prevents
stragglers from holding up the system without wasting the work that stragglers
can complete. We present a convergence analysis and analyze the wall time
performance. Our numerical results show that our approach is up to 1.5 times
faster in Amazon EC2 and it is up to five times faster when there is greater
variability in compute node performance.
Rewrite this for me:
Distributed optimization is essential for tackling large-scale machine learning tasks. A common characteristic of these methods is their synchronous nature: every computational node must finish its work within an epoch before the system can advance. This makes the overall speed vulnerable to lagging nodes, known as stragglers, which can severely impede progress.

To address this inefficiency, we introduce **Anytime Minibatch**, an online distributed optimization technique. Instead of assigning a fixed workload, our method allocates a fixed computation window to each node. Within this time, nodes process as many data samples as they can, leading to a variable, node-specific minibatch size. Subsequently, workers have a fixed communication period to perform several rounds of consensus, averaging their computed minibatch gradients. These averaged gradients are then used to update the primal variables through dual averaging.

This design ensures that stragglers no longer bottleneck the system, while still utilizing all the work they complete. We provide a theoretical convergence analysis and a practical assessment of wall-clock performance. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that Anytime Minibatch achieves speed-ups of up to 1.5 times in an Amazon EC2 environment, and up to five times faster in scenarios with high variability in node performance.

Scaling end-to-end reinforcement learning to control real robots from vision
presents a series of challenges, in particular in terms of sample efficiency.
Against end-to-end learning, state representation learning can help learn a
compact, efficient and relevant representation of states that speeds up policy
learning, reducing the number of samples needed, and that is easier to
interpret. We evaluate several state representation learning methods on goal
based robotics tasks and propose a new unsupervised model that stacks
representations and combines strengths of several of these approaches. This
method encodes all the relevant features, performs on par or better than
end-to-end learning with better sample efficiency, and is robust to
hyper-parameters change.
Rewrite this for me:
Training robots with end-to-end reinforcement learning, using only visual input, is hindered by poor sample efficiency. State representation learning offers a solution by extracting a compact and meaningful description of the environment. This learned representation accelerates policy training, reduces the required data, and improves interpretability compared to raw pixels. We assess multiple representation learning techniques on robotic goal tasks and introduce a novel unsupervised model. It stacks representations, merging the advantages of different methods. Our approach encodes all necessary features, matches or surpasses end-to-end learning performance with greater sample efficiency, and maintains robustness across hyperparameter variations.

A central challenge in reinforcement learning is discovering effective
policies for tasks where rewards are sparsely distributed. We postulate that in
the absence of useful reward signals, an effective exploration strategy should
seek out {\it decision states}. These states lie at critical junctions in the
state space from where the agent can transition to new, potentially unexplored
regions. We propose to learn about decision states from prior experience. By
training a goal-conditioned policy with an information bottleneck, we can
identify decision states by examining where the model actually leverages the
goal state. We find that this simple mechanism effectively identifies decision
states, even in partially observed settings. In effect, the model learns the
sensory cues that correlate with potential subgoals. In new environments, this
model can then identify novel subgoals for further exploration, guiding the
agent through a sequence of potential decision states and through new regions
of the state space.
Rewrite this for me:
A core difficulty in reinforcement learning is finding good policies when rewards are scarce. We argue that without clear reward signals, a successful exploration strategy must seek out *decision states*—critical junctures in the state space from which an agent can branch into new, possibly unknown regions. Our method learns to recognize these states from prior experience. We train a goal-conditioned policy using an information bottleneck; decision states are then revealed as points where the model meaningfully uses the goal information. This straightforward approach reliably identifies decision states, even under partial observability. Essentially, the model learns the sensory cues that signal potential subgoals. When placed in a new environment, it can detect novel subgoals to drive exploration, steering the agent through a series of decision states and into uncharted areas of the state space.

input:
Multilingual machine translation, which translates multiple languages with a
single model, has attracted much attention due to its efficiency of offline
training and online serving. However, traditional multilingual translation
usually yields inferior accuracy compared with the counterpart using individual
models for each language pair, due to language diversity and model capacity
limitations. In this paper, we propose a distillation-based approach to boost
the accuracy of multilingual machine translation. Specifically, individual
models are first trained and regarded as teachers, and then the multilingual
model is trained to fit the training data and match the outputs of individual
models simultaneously through knowledge distillation. Experiments on IWSLT, WMT
and Ted talk translation datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.
Particularly, we show that one model is enough to handle multiple languages (up
to 44 languages in our experiment), with comparable or even better accuracy
than individual models.
Rewrite this for me:
Multilingual machine translation uses a single model to translate between many languages, offering greater efficiency in both training and deployment than maintaining separate models for each language pair. However, this approach has traditionally suffered from lower accuracy, a consequence of language diversity and limited model capacity.

To address this, we propose a method that enhances multilingual translation accuracy through knowledge distillation. First, we train high-performance individual models for specific language pairs to act as "teachers." Then, we train the single multilingual "student" model not only on standard training data but also to replicate the outputs of these teacher models. This distillation process transfers refined knowledge to the unified model.

Experiments on IWSLT, WMT, and TED talk datasets confirm our method's effectiveness. We demonstrate that one model can capably handle many languages—up to 44 in our tests—achieving accuracy that is comparable to, and sometimes surpasses, that of individual dedicated models.

We introduce PyTorch Geometric, a library for deep learning on irregularly
structured input data such as graphs, point clouds and manifolds, built upon
PyTorch. In addition to general graph data structures and processing methods,
it contains a variety of recently published methods from the domains of
relational learning and 3D data processing. PyTorch Geometric achieves high
data throughput by leveraging sparse GPU acceleration, by providing dedicated
CUDA kernels and by introducing efficient mini-batch handling for input
examples of different size. In this work, we present the library in detail and
perform a comprehensive comparative study of the implemented methods in
homogeneous evaluation scenarios.
Rewrite this for me: PyTorch Geometric is a PyTorch-based library designed for deep learning on non-Euclidean data, including graphs, point clouds, and manifolds. It provides general graph data structures and processing tools, alongside a collection of recent techniques from relational learning and 3D data analysis. The library ensures high performance through sparse GPU acceleration, custom CUDA kernels, and efficient mini-batch processing for variably-sized inputs. This paper offers a detailed overview of PyTorch Geometric and conducts an extensive comparative evaluation of its methods under uniform experimental conditions.

Although variational autoencoders (VAEs) represent a widely influential deep
generative model, many aspects of the underlying energy function remain poorly
understood. In particular, it is commonly believed that Gaussian
encoder/decoder assumptions reduce the effectiveness of VAEs in generating
realistic samples. In this regard, we rigorously analyze the VAE objective,
differentiating situations where this belief is and is not actually true. We
then leverage the corresponding insights to develop a simple VAE enhancement
that requires no additional hyperparameters or sensitive tuning.
Quantitatively, this proposal produces crisp samples and stable FID scores that
are actually competitive with a variety of GAN models, all while retaining
desirable attributes of the original VAE architecture. A shorter version of
this work will appear in the ICLR 2019 conference proceedings (Dai and Wipf,
2019). The code for our model is available at https://github.com/daib13/
TwoStageVAE.
Rewrite this for me:
While variational autoencoders (VAEs) are a prominent deep generative model, key properties of their underlying energy function are not fully understood. A common view holds that the standard Gaussian assumptions for the encoder and decoder limit the model’s ability to produce realistic samples. This work provides a rigorous analysis of the VAE objective, clarifying when this belief holds and when it does not. Building on these insights, we introduce a straightforward enhancement to the VAE that requires no extra hyperparameters or delicate tuning. The resulting model generates sharp samples and achieves stable Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) scores competitive with several GAN variants, while preserving the desirable features of the original VAE. A condensed version will appear at ICLR 2019 (Dai & Wipf, 2019). Code is available at: https://github.com/daib13/TwoStageVAE.

input:
Adversarial training is a training scheme designed to counter adversarial
attacks by augmenting the training dataset with adversarial examples.
Surprisingly, several studies have observed that loss gradients from
adversarially trained DNNs are visually more interpretable than those from
standard DNNs. Although this phenomenon is interesting, there are only few
works that have offered an explanation. In this paper, we attempted to bridge
this gap between adversarial robustness and gradient interpretability. To this
end, we identified that loss gradients from adversarially trained DNNs align
better with human perception because adversarial training restricts gradients
closer to the image manifold. We then demonstrated that adversarial training
causes loss gradients to be quantitatively meaningful. Finally, we showed that
under the adversarial training framework, there exists an empirical trade-off
between test accuracy and loss gradient interpretability and proposed two
potential approaches to resolving this trade-off.
Rewrite this for me:
Adversarial training strengthens neural networks against attacks by including adversarial examples in their training data. Interestingly, research has shown that the loss gradients from these robust models are also more visually interpretable to humans than those from standard models. While notable, this link between robustness and interpretability has lacked a clear explanation.

Our work addresses this gap. We find that adversarial training constrains gradients to align more closely with the true image manifold, which inherently aligns them better with human perception. We demonstrate that this results in quantitatively meaningful gradients. Furthermore, we reveal an empirical trade-off within this framework: increasing gradient interpretability can come at the cost of test accuracy. We conclude by proposing two potential methods to help mitigate this trade-off.

In this work we show preliminary results of deep multi-task learning in the
area of computational pathology. We combine 11 tasks ranging from patch-wise
oral cancer classification, one of the most prevalent cancers in the developing

input:
The principle of compositionality, which enables natural language to
represent complex concepts via a structured combination of simpler ones, allows
us to convey an open-ended set of messages using a limited vocabulary. If
compositionality is indeed a natural property of language, we may expect it to
appear in communication protocols that are created by neural agents in language
games. In this paper, we propose an effective neural iterated learning (NIL)
algorithm that, when applied to interacting neural agents, facilitates the
emergence of a more structured type of language. Indeed, these languages
provide learning speed advantages to neural agents during training, which can
be incrementally amplified via NIL. We provide a probabilistic model of NIL and
an explanation of why the advantage of compositional language exist. Our
experiments confirm our analysis, and also demonstrate that the emerged
languages largely improve the generalizing power of the neural agent
communication.
Rewrite this for me:
The principle of compositionality allows natural language to express an open-ended range of complex ideas by systematically combining a finite set of simpler elements. If this is a fundamental property of language, we should anticipate its emergence in communication protocols developed by neural agents engaged in language games.

This paper introduces an effective neural iterated learning (NIL) algorithm. When applied to interacting neural agents, NIL promotes the development of a more structured, compositional language. Such languages offer agents a significant learning speed advantage during training, an advantage that NIL can incrementally amplify. We present a probabilistic model of NIL and explain the source of this compositional advantage.

Our experimental results confirm this analysis and show that the emerged languages substantially enhance the generalization capability of neural agent communication.

input:
Text generation is ubiquitous in many NLP tasks, from summarization, to
dialogue and machine translation. The dominant parametric approach is based on
locally normalized models which predict one word at a time. While these work
remarkably well, they are plagued by exposure bias due to the greedy nature of
the generation process. In this work, we investigate un-normalized energy-based
models (EBMs) which operate not at the token but at the sequence level. In
order to make training tractable, we first work in the residual of a pretrained
locally normalized language model and second we train using noise contrastive
estimation. Furthermore, since the EBM works at the sequence level, we can
leverage pretrained bi-directional contextual representations, such as BERT and
RoBERTa. Our experiments on two large language modeling datasets show that
residual EBMs yield lower perplexity compared to locally normalized baselines.
Moreover, generation via importance sampling is very efficient and of higher
quality than the baseline models according to human evaluation.
Rewrite this for me:
Text generation is central to many NLP applications, including summarization, dialogue, and machine translation. The prevailing parametric method relies on locally normalized models that predict words sequentially. Although highly effective, these models suffer from exposure bias, a consequence of their greedy, step-by-step generation.

This work explores an alternative: un-normalized energy-based models (EBMs) that operate at the full sequence level, rather than token-by-token. To ensure tractable training, we employ two key strategies. First, we model the residual of a pretrained local language model. Second, we utilize noise contrastive estimation. Because EBMs assess entire sequences, they can directly leverage powerful pretrained bidirectional representations like BERT and RoBERTa.

Experiments on two major language modeling datasets demonstrate that our residual EBMs achieve lower perplexity than standard locally normalized baselines. Furthermore, generation through importance sampling proves both efficient and superior in quality, as confirmed by human evaluation.

We propose an energy-based model (EBM) of protein conformations that operates
at atomic scale. The model is trained solely on crystallized protein data. By
contrast, existing approaches for scoring conformations use energy functions
that incorporate knowledge of physical principles and features that are the
complex product of several decades of research and tuning. To evaluate the
model, we benchmark on the rotamer recovery task, the problem of predicting the
conformation of a side chain from its context within a protein structure, which
has been used to evaluate energy functions for protein design. The model
achieves performance close to that of the Rosetta energy function, a
state-of-the-art method widely used in protein structure prediction and design.
An investigation of the model's outputs and hidden representations finds that
it captures physicochemical properties relevant to protein energy.
Rewrite this for me: We propose an atomic-scale energy-based model (EBM) for protein conformations, trained exclusively on crystallized protein data. This contrasts with established methods, which rely on energy functions built from decades of research into physical principles and carefully tuned features. For evaluation, we use the rotamer recovery task—predicting a side chain's conformation from its structural context—a standard benchmark for protein design energy functions. Our model performs nearly on par with the widely-used, state-of-the-art Rosetta energy function. Further analysis reveals that the model’s outputs and internal representations successfully capture key physicochemical properties relevant to protein energy.

We prove that the reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) of a deep neural
tangent kernel and the Laplace kernel include the same set of functions, when
both kernels are restricted to the sphere $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Additionally, we
prove that the exponential power kernel with a smaller power (making the kernel
less smooth) leads to a larger RKHS, when it is restricted to the sphere
$\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ and when it is defined on the entire $\mathbb{R}^d$.
Rewrite this for me:
We show that the reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) for a deep neural tangent kernel and the Laplace kernel contain identical functions when both are restricted to the sphere \(\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\). Furthermore, we prove that for the exponential power kernel, a smaller power (resulting in a less smooth kernel) yields a larger RKHS, both on the sphere \(\mathbb{S}^{d-1}\) and on all of \(\mathbb{R}^d\).

input:
We study training of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with ReLU
activations and introduce exact convex optimization formulations with a
polynomial complexity with respect to the number of data samples, the number of
neurons, and data dimension. More specifically, we develop a convex analytic
framework utilizing semi-infinite duality to obtain equivalent convex
optimization problems for several two- and three-layer CNN architectures. We
first prove that two-layer CNNs can be globally optimized via an $\ell_2$ norm
regularized convex program. We then show that multi-layer circular CNN training
problems with a single ReLU layer are equivalent to an $\ell_1$ regularized
convex program that encourages sparsity in the spectral domain. We also extend
these results to three-layer CNNs with two ReLU layers. Furthermore, we present
extensions of our approach to different pooling methods, which elucidates the
implicit architectural bias as convex regularizers.
Rewrite this for me:
We investigate the training of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) that use ReLU activation functions. Our work introduces exact convex optimization formulations for this process, where the computational complexity scales polynomially with the dataset size, neuron count, and data dimensionality. Using a convex analytic framework based on semi-infinite duality, we derive equivalent convex problems for various two- and three-layer CNN architectures.

We first establish that training a two-layer CNN is equivalent to a globally solvable convex program regularized by the ℓ₂ norm. For multi-layer circular CNNs with one ReLU layer, we prove equivalence to an ℓ₁-regularized convex problem, promoting sparsity in the spectral domain. These findings are extended to three-layer networks containing two ReLU layers. Additionally, we adapt our approach to various pooling methods, revealing that the associated architectural choices function as specific convex regularizers.

We propose a new metric space of ReLU activation codes equipped with a
truncated Hamming distance which establishes an isometry between its elements
and polyhedral bodies in the input space which have recently been shown to be
strongly related to safety, robustness, and confidence. This isometry allows
the efficient computation of adjacency relations between the polyhedral bodies.
Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 indicate that information besides accuracy
might be stored in the code space.

This creates an isometry between the codes and polyhedral regions in the input space, regions linked to model safety, robustness, and confidence. The isometry enables efficient calculation of adjacencies between these polyhedral bodies. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 suggest the code space may contain information beyond just predictive accuracy.

This paper introduces the first dataset of satellite images labeled with
forage quality by on-the-ground experts and provides proof of concept for
applying computer vision methods to index-based drought insurance. We also
present the results of a collaborative benchmark tool used to crowdsource an
accurate machine learning model on the dataset. Our methods significantly
outperform the existing technology for an insurance program in Northern Kenya,
suggesting that a computer vision-based approach could substantially benefit
pastoralists, whose exposure to droughts is severe and worsening with climate
change.

This indicates that a computer vision-based method could greatly aid pastoralists, whose severe vulnerability to drought is intensifying with climate change.

Recent advances in neural machine translation (NMT) have led to
state-of-the-art results for many European-based translation tasks. However,
despite these advances, there is has been little focus in applying these
methods to African languages. In this paper, we seek to address this gap by
creating an NMT benchmark BLEU score between English and the ten remaining
official languages in South Africa.

This paper addresses that gap by establishing a benchmark of BLEU scores for translations between English and South Africa's ten other official languages.

With the recent success and popularity of pre-trained language models (LMs)
in natural language processing, there has been a rise in efforts to understand
their inner workings. In line with such interest, we propose a novel method
that assists us in investigating the extent to which pre-trained LMs capture
the syntactic notion of constituency. Our method provides an effective way of
extracting constituency trees from the pre-trained LMs without training. In
addition, we report intriguing findings in the induced trees, including the
fact that pre-trained LMs outperform other approaches in correctly demarcating
adverb phrases in sentences.
Rewrite this for me: The growing success of pre-trained language models (LMs) has spurred efforts to understand their internal mechanisms. In this context, we introduce a novel method for investigating how well these models capture syntactic constituency. Our approach enables the extraction of constituency trees directly from pre-trained LMs, requiring no additional training. The induced trees reveal intriguing results, notably that pre-trained LMs excel at correctly identifying adverb phrase boundaries, outperforming other established methods.

Magnitude-based pruning is one of the simplest methods for pruning neural
networks. Despite its simplicity, magnitude-based pruning and its variants
demonstrated remarkable performances for pruning modern architectures. Based on
the observation that magnitude-based pruning indeed minimizes the Frobenius
distortion of a linear operator corresponding to a single layer, we develop a
simple pruning method, coined lookahead pruning, by extending the single layer
optimization to a multi-layer optimization. Our experimental results
demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms magnitude-based
pruning on various networks, including VGG and ResNet, particularly in the
high-sparsity regime. See https://github.com/alinlab/lookahead_pruning for
codes.
Rewrite this for me:
Magnitude-based pruning is a simple yet effective technique for compressing neural networks. Noting that it minimizes the Frobenius distortion for a single layer, we extend this principle to a multi-layer optimization. This leads to our proposed method, lookahead pruning. Experiments show it consistently surpasses standard magnitude-based pruning across networks like VGG and ResNet, especially at high sparsity levels. Code is available at https://github.com/alinlab/lookahead_pruning.

As the share of renewable energy sources in the present electric energy mix
rises, their intermittence proves to be the biggest challenge to carbon free
electricity generation. To address this challenge, we propose an electricity
pricing agent, which sends price signals to the customers and contributes to
shifting the customer demand to periods of high renewable energy generation. We
propose an implementation of a pricing agent with a reinforcement learning
approach where the environment is represented by the customers, the electricity
generation utilities and the weather conditions.

This agent sends dynamic price signals to consumers, incentivizing them to shift their demand toward periods of high renewable generation. We implement this agent using a reinforcement learning approach, where the environment is modeled by customer behavior, power generation utilities, and weather conditions.

Nigerian Pidgin is arguably the most widely spoken language in Nigeria.
Variants of this language are also spoken across West and Central Africa,
making it a very important language. This work aims to establish supervised and
unsupervised neural machine translation (NMT) baselines between English and
Nigerian Pidgin. We implement and compare NMT models with different
tokenization methods, creating a solid foundation for future works.

input:
Estimating grape yield prior to harvest is important to commercial vineyard
production as it informs many vineyard and winery decisions. Currently, the
process of yield estimation is time consuming and varies in its accuracy from
75-90\% depending on the experience of the viticulturist. This paper proposes a
multiple task learning (MTL) convolutional neural network (CNN) approach that
uses images captured by inexpensive smart phones secured in a simple tripod
arrangement. The CNN models use MTL transfer from autoencoders to achieve 85\%
accuracy from image data captured 6 days prior to harvest.
Rewrite this for me: Accurate pre-harvest grape yield estimation is vital for guiding vineyard and winery operations. Current methods, however, are labor-intensive and achieve variable accuracy, typically between 75% and 90%, depending heavily on the viticulturist's skill. This paper introduces a method using a multi-task learning (MTL) convolutional neural network (CNN). The system analyzes images taken with affordable smartphones mounted on simple tripods just six days before harvest. By employing transfer learning from autoencoders, the model attains a consistent 85% prediction accuracy.

input:
Automatic change detection and disaster damage assessment are currently
procedures requiring a huge amount of labor and manual work by satellite
imagery analysts. In the occurrences of natural disasters, timely change
detection can save lives. In this work, we report findings on problem framing,
data processing and training procedures which are specifically helpful for the
task of building damage assessment using the newly released xBD dataset. Our
insights lead to substantial improvement over the xBD baseline models, and we
score among top results on the xView2 challenge leaderboard. We release our
code used for the competition.

Automated change detection and disaster damage assessment currently demand extensive manual effort from satellite imagery analysts. During natural disasters, timely detection can save lives. This work details effective approaches to problem framing, data processing, and model training specifically for building damage assessment, using the new xBD dataset. Our methods yield significant improvements over the xBD baseline models and achieve competitive results on the xView2 challenge leaderboard. The code developed for this competition is publicly released.

input:
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are non-linear dynamic systems. Previous
work believes that RNN may suffer from the phenomenon of chaos, where the
system is sensitive to initial states and unpredictable in the long run. In
this paper, however, we perform a systematic empirical analysis, showing that a
vanilla or long short term memory (LSTM) RNN does not exhibit chaotic behavior
along the training process in real applications such as text generation. Our
findings suggest that future work in this direction should address the other
side of non-linear dynamics for RNN.
Rewrite this for me: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are non-linear dynamic systems. Prior research has suggested they may exhibit chaotic behavior, characterized by extreme sensitivity to initial conditions and long-term unpredictability. This paper presents a systematic empirical analysis demonstrating that, in practical applications like text generation, neither standard nor LSTM RNNs display such chaos during training. Our results indicate that future investigations should instead focus on other aspects of non-linear dynamics within RNNs.

input:
Fine-tuning a pretrained BERT model is the state of the art method for
extractive/abstractive text summarization, in this paper we showcase how this
fine-tuning method can be applied to the Arabic language to both construct the
first documented model for abstractive Arabic text summarization and show its
performance in Arabic extractive summarization. Our model works with
multilingual BERT (as Arabic language does not have a pretrained BERT of its
own). We show its performance in English corpus first before applying it to
Arabic corpora in both extractive and abstractive tasks.
Rewrite this for me:
This paper demonstrates how fine-tuning a pretrained BERT model—the established method for text summarization—can be applied to Arabic. Since no dedicated Arabic BERT exists, we utilize multilingual BERT. We first validate the model's performance on an English corpus. We then apply it to Arabic corpora for both extractive and abstractive summarization, thereby creating the first documented model for abstractive Arabic text summarization and reporting its extractive summarization results.

input:
During cluster analysis domain experts and visual analysis are frequently
relied on to identify the optimal clustering structure. This process tends to
be adhoc, subjective and difficult to reproduce. This work shows how competency
questions can be used to formalise expert knowledge and application
requirements for context specific evaluation of a clustering application in the
residential energy consumption sector.
Rewrite this for me: In cluster analysis, experts and visual methods are often used to find the best structure, but this process is typically ad-hoc, subjective, and hard to reproduce. This work demonstrates how competency questions can formalize expert knowledge and application needs, enabling a context-specific evaluation for a residential energy consumption clustering application.

input:
Action and observation delays commonly occur in many Reinforcement Learning
applications, such as remote control scenarios. We study the anatomy of
randomly delayed environments, and show that partially resampling trajectory
fragments in hindsight allows for off-policy multi-step value estimation. We
apply this principle to derive Delay-Correcting Actor-Critic (DCAC), an
algorithm based on Soft Actor-Critic with significantly better performance in
environments with delays. This is shown theoretically and also demonstrated
practically on a delay-augmented version of the MuJoCo continuous control
benchmark.
Rewrite this for me: Action and observation delays are frequent in Reinforcement Learning, especially in remote control. We analyze randomly delayed environments and demonstrate that partially resampling past trajectory fragments enables effective off-policy, multi-step value estimation. Applying this insight, we develop Delay-Correcting Actor-Critic (DCAC). Built on Soft Actor-Critic, DCAC achieves substantially better performance in delayed settings, a result we prove theoretically and validate empirically on a delayed version of the MuJoCo continuous control benchmark.

input:
We demonstrate that differentially private machine learning has not yet
reached its "AlexNet moment" on many canonical vision tasks: linear models
trained on handcrafted features significantly outperform end-to-end deep neural
networks for moderate privacy budgets. To exceed the performance of handcrafted
features, we show that private learning requires either much more private data,
or access to features learned on public data from a similar domain. Our work
introduces simple yet strong baselines for differentially private learning that
can inform the evaluation of future progress in this area.
Rewrite this for me: Our findings show that differentially private machine learning has not yet achieved a breakthrough moment on standard vision tasks. For moderate privacy budgets, linear models using handcrafted features still surpass end-to-end deep neural networks. To outperform these handcrafted features, private learning needs substantially more private data, or access to relevant features pre-trained on public data. This work establishes simple but strong baselines to better guide and evaluate future progress in private learning.

Anomaly detection, finding patterns that substantially deviate from those
seen previously, is one of the fundamental problems of artificial intelligence.
Recently, classification-based methods were shown to achieve superior results
on this task. In this work, we present a unifying view and propose an open-set
method, GOAD, to relax current generalization assumptions. Furthermore, we
extend the applicability of transformation-based methods to non-image data
using random affine transformations. Our method is shown to obtain
state-of-the-art accuracy and is applicable to broad data types. The strong
performance of our method is extensively validated on multiple datasets from
different domains.
Rewrite this for me: Anomaly detection, which identifies patterns that significantly differ from established norms, is a core challenge in artificial intelligence. While recent classification-based approaches have delivered leading results, this work introduces a unifying perspective. We propose GOAD, an open-set method that relaxes current generalization constraints. Additionally, we expand the use of transformation-based techniques to non-image data via random affine transformations. Demonstrated to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy across diverse data types, our method's robust performance is thoroughly validated on multiple datasets from various domains.

In this paper, we cast fair machine learning as invariant machine learning.
We first formulate a version of individual fairness that enforces invariance on
certain sensitive sets. We then design a transport-based regularizer that
enforces this version of individual fairness and develop an algorithm to
minimize the regularizer efficiently. Our theoretical results guarantee the
proposed approach trains certifiably fair ML models. Finally, in the
experimental studies we demonstrate improved fairness metrics in comparison to
several recent fair training procedures on three ML tasks that are susceptible
to algorithmic bias.
Rewrite this for me:
This paper reframes fair machine learning as a problem of achieving invariance. We propose a formulation of individual fairness that requires model predictions to remain stable within specific sensitive groups. To enforce this, we design a transport-based regularization method and develop an efficient algorithm for its optimization. Theoretically, our approach guarantees the training of certifiably fair models. Experiments across three bias-prone tasks show that our method improves key fairness metrics compared to several recent fair training procedures.

Despite significant advances, continual learning models still suffer from
catastrophic forgetting when exposed to incrementally available data from
non-stationary distributions. Rehearsal approaches alleviate the problem by
maintaining and replaying a small episodic memory of previous samples, often
implemented as an array of independent memory slots. In this work, we propose
to augment such an array with a learnable random graph that captures pairwise
similarities between its samples, and use it not only to learn new tasks but
also to guard against forgetting. Empirical results on several benchmark
datasets show that our model consistently outperforms recently proposed
baselines for task-free continual learning.
Rewrite this for me: Continual learning models have progressed, yet they remain vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting when processing sequential data from shifting distributions. Rehearsal methods counter this by storing and replaying a compact episodic memory, typically structured as a simple array of independent samples. We enhance this approach by integrating a learnable random graph into the memory array. This graph models pairwise relationships between stored samples, enabling the system to leverage these connections both for acquiring new knowledge and for actively protecting previous learning. Evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our method reliably surpasses recent baselines in task-free continual learning.
